speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members of the house would want me to direct their attention to the fact that in the diplomatic gallery there is a parliamentary delegation from the house of representatives of the Federation of Nigeria. The delegation composed of eight parliamentary members is under the leadership of Chief Oweh, parliamentary secretary to the minister of internal affairs. Their visit is one of a continuing series of visits first to the United Kingdom, now to Canada and later to the United States of America, and their purpose is the study of the parliamentary institutions in those countries.
I am sure I speak for all hon. members in welcoming them, and in expressing the hope that their stay in our midst will be profitable and enjoyable.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: WELCOME TO VISITORS IN GALLERY FROM NIGERIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our party I should simply like to join the Prime Minister in the very fitting and warm welcome he has extended to the distinguished representatives of a sister country in our commonwealth.

maintopic: WELCOME TO VISITORS IN GALLERY FROM NIGERIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate hon. members of this group with the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition in welcoming this very distinguished group of members of the house of representatives of Nigeria.
My colleague from Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and I had the privilege of having lunch with them, and we learned a great deal at lunch time about the workings of democracy in this new nation which is part of the commonwealth. We learned from them that they share some of our experience, in that they are looking forward to an election in that country within the next two years and, being a democracy, they are looking forward to that election with keen interest. It is a real pleasure for us to see Nigeria taking its place amongst the democratic nations of the world, and we wish these representatives and their nation the best in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the President and the Secretary of State of the United States have indicated in some detail the nature of the visit they are making to Ottawa and the subjects that will be discussed, and in view of the fact that the Prime Minister himself made a statement about this over the air last night, would he

Inquiries of the Ministry now inform the house as to the nature of the visit and perhaps in a general way the subjects that may be discussed?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SUBJECTS TO BE DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I say that Canadians as a whole are looking forward with anticipation to the visit of the President of the United States, renewing, as he will, the relationships which were so close during the days of war, and also on this occasion renewing the friendships that he made on previous occasions, first when he was here immediately after the war and then again in November, 1953, when he addressed members of parliament.
I think in general one might summarize those discussions as being informal, designed to achieve an exchange of views between our countries. There will be no set agenda, as I am sure my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition will realize, but of course consideration will be given to various matters which are of immediate interest and importance, both internationally and nationally.
In the international field I would expect an exchange of views regarding the present situation as between the free world and the U.S.S.R.; consideration of the question as to summit talks and the possibility of those talks being inaugurated; the general subject of disarmament with particular reference to our own country and collaboration existing between Canada and the United States, and the matter of Arctic inspection.
Then, too, in the economic field I would anticipate that there would be very considerable attention paid to the economic offensive of the U.S.S.R. everywhere in the world, the effect of which, unless there is a large degree of co-operation among the member nations of the free world, might be apt to be detrimental to that degree of unity so necessary today.
In so far as our relationship with the United States directly is concerned, trading problems will of necessity receive consideration. In that connection I would consider that some of those matters that have received the attention of members of the government, as well as those dealt with in recent speeches by the Leader of the Opposition, will be of foremost importance. The disposal of surplus wheat and other agricultural products by the United States is one matter, of course, that will again receive consideration. The marketing of Canadian oil in the United States is another. The question of the export of zinc and copper to the United States is another. I would also think that aluminum and nickel are two other commodities to which reference will be made and representations considered.

Personally I should like to see agreements arrived at whereby there would be a more continuous exchange of information on cabinet level than has been the case heretofore; in other words, that the joint United States-Canadian cabinet committee should meet more regularly. Indeed, I feel that once a year is insufficient to assure that full discussion and consideration which the economic problems between our countries deserve and demand. My hope is that consideration will be given to the setting up of an informal committee of members of parliament and members of the congress of the United States, to the end that in meeting together from time to time many of the problems which are difficult of solution will be accelerated toward solution by each of us realizing the problems of the other country.
In short, the purpose of this meeting as I envisage it is simply one of exchange of opinions and, above all, that each of us will do our respective part to resolve any difficulties that exist from time to time between our countries. I hope that agreements to be arrived at will be beneficial not only to our own countries but to the maintenance of freedom everywhere in the world.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN AGREEMENT AS TO USE FOR DEFENCE PURPOSES
speechtext:
On Friday last the Leader of the Opposition addressed this question to me:
In view of the pattern of three-power co-operation developed during world war II on atomic matters, could the minister inform the house whether Canada will be invited to join in the agreement signed, I think, the day before yesterday between the United Kingdom and the United States for co-operation on the use of atomic energy for defence purposes?
If I may quote the words of the Prime Minister, that request was too comprehensive for me at the time and I took it as notice. The simple answer to the question is that Canada, while kept informed of developments by both London and Washington, did not join in what according to my understanding is a bilateral agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States. It is true that there was tripartite co-operation during the war on atomic energy matters, and I feel confident that such co-operation would be reactivated if and when necessary.
Since the war, however, co-operation with the United States in this field has for the most part assumed a bilateral form. As the Leader of the Opposition will undoubtedly recall, Canada and the United Kingdom have had bilateral agreements with the United States in the atomic energy field, both civil and military, for some years. My understanding is

Inquiries of the Ministry that the United Kingdom requirements, which are different from Canadian requirements, are such as to call for a new agreement at this time between those two countries.
The new agreement has been made possible by recent amendments to the atomic energy act authorizing congress to expand the areas in which United States information could be given to a friendly country which has made substantial progress in the development of atomic weapons. When and if Canadian requirements call for a supplementary agreement with the United States, the house can assume that a similar course will no doubt be followed. Canada at this time does not qualify for that type of agreement prescribed by the amendments to the atomic energy act of the United States congress.
