speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion gives me an opportunity to raise a matter of very great importance, namely a national development policy, and at the conclusion of my remarks to move an amendment concerning it. I hope to deal with this matter myself in fairly general terms, and subsequently my colleagues who are participating in this debate will deal with somewhat more detailed matters arising out of the question.
In a young and rapidly growing country like Canada-and we are young and rapidly growing-it is essential to have a flexible national development policy adapted to the changing needs of our people. If indeed flexibility in this field is not preserved, if the aims and contents of our national development policy do not rest upon a systematic national assessment of our changing economic and social requirements, overexpansion may result in certain sectors and certain regions while others may suffer from stagnation and underdevelopment. In other words, unevenness of economic development is a major danger to our economy. Indeed, our history shows that it is also a danger to our unity.
It would be useful in opening this discussion, I think to review very briefly the historical evolution of our national development policy which, as I see it, has been marked by three distinct periods. The first, of course, is the Macdonald era, from 1867 to, I suppose, about 1895. It was characterized by the acquisition of Rupert's land and the Northwest Territories, by the construction of railways and canals and the implementation of the national policy in 1878. In spite of the unfavourable impact of that policy on our maritime provinces, the aims and contents of the policy in other respects were, I think, adapted to the economic circumstances of that period. Indeed, it was essential at that time to create an economic frontier and for that purpose to provide

National Development Policy transcontinental transportation facilities which were of vital importance not only economically but also politically.
Nevertheless, in spite of what I think we might fairly term Sir John A. Macdonald's dynamic-and, if you like, imaginative- policy, economic development throughout that period was very slow. It has been estimated that over one million Canadians emigrated to the United States from 1860 to 1890. Yet I think we must all recognize, wherever we may sit in the house and whatever our political views may be, that the basis for our future growth was laid during that period. The Canadian people, I am sure, will always admire and be grateful to Sir John A. for his great vision and his great achievements despite the unfavourable economic climate of that time.
Then from the end of that period, 1896, to the great depression of the 1930's we had, I think, another period in our national development, a period during which of course there was no uninterrupted succession of Liberal governments because we had the government of another great Canadian, Sir Robert Borden, during that time and we also had the first world war. I think, however, it is not unfair to characterize that second period as the Sir Wilfrid Laurier-Mackenzie King era.
That was a very great and active period in our history marked by the opening up and the settlement of the west. During that time wheat production became complementary to the manufacturing production of the east and indeed, I suppose, during those years it is not an exaggeration to say that wheat dominated the economic scene. It became of vital importance in our international balance of payments; and the wheat economy, the opening up of the west, became of very great importance also in providing a market for the manufactures of the east.
That period perhaps came to an end in 1930, with the transfer of natural resources to the provinces and the great depression of that decade. During that decade of the 1930's-we all remember those years-the country was preoccupied with getting out of the depression; and then came the second world war, when main emphasis of course had to be placed on defence and indeed on survival.
During those two earlier periods our national development policy was, I think, bold and imaginative; but we must not forget, especially in regard to the problems of the present and what we should do about them, that that policy often lacked proper balance and that occasionally it put the emphasis in the wrong direction, with the result that at times we were overextended 
or, if you like, overequipped in certain sectors and that we perhaps unnecessarily imposed some heavy overhead burdens on the Canadian economy.
The principal of Queen's, Dr. Mackintosh, for instance, has written about our railway policy in those years; that it had been fantastically optimistic and misdirected. It is generally recognized that some areas in the west which were developed during those periods should not have been devoted to wheat production. Our overexpansion in certain fields unduly increased our overhead costs generally in this country and also prevented us from promoting more desirable projects perhaps in other sectors or regions of the nation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we come to the third great period in our development, which coincided with the years after world war II. We still remembered then the achievements of the earlier years, but we also coupled with those achievements, as any government I think was bound to do, some of the miscalculations of the past. I maintain that our national development policy during those years after world war II was vigorous, constructive and successful, in spite of heavy public expenditures for defence, unprecedented in our history in peacetime, and in spite of very heavy expenditures for social security. But our development policy during those years was not only vigorous; it was, I think, somewhat better balanced and better planned than it had been before.
Perhaps the main new element in this third period of development was the greater impetus given during those years to the opening up of the northern economic frontier. New transportation facilities weTe made available for that purpose by the federal government, or with its assistance or permission. I am not going to detain the house, Mr. Speaker, by going into the detailed record of transportation developments during those years; it is there for all to see, and I know that hon. members are aware of it. There was not only road transportation and rail transportation to northern areas, but right across the country there was a vast program of airport construction carried on in the northern part of our territory.
Then we recall that in 1953 a new federal Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources was set up in recognition of the growing importance of our northern regions. Under able and energetic leadership that new department took a very active interest not only in economic development of that vast territory but also in the greater well-being of its population.

The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources also gave active consideration to the planning of long-term development in the north. This did not begin last year, Mr. Speaker; it began when this department was set up, and only two years after the creation of the department, at the end of 1955, the department presented, through the commissioners of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, two briefs to the Gordon commission outlining long-term plans for the next 25 years, the implementation of which had begun at that time. These are the two briefs which were presented to the Gordon commission at that time and which provided the basis for planning and development in the Arctic, planning and development which had indeed begun.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these two briefs also formed the basis of the famous vision that we heard so much about during the election campaign. However, during that time we did not hear any mention of the fact that this vision was merely an adapted version of a plan which had been drawn up a few years before and which was being implemented. After the election, however, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources did state-and not very long ago, a few days ago-that there was nothing new in the content of the vision except that the implementation of the Liberal plan on which it was based was speeded up.
I shall come back to that point later, Mr. Speaker. For the moment I just want to say that the Liberal party is proud of its post-war record in the north, both in terms of realization and in terms of planning for the future, but I would add-and this is important to get the matter in perspective-that our national development policy when we were in power was not merely centred on northern development. During the post-war period an impressive program was initiated in the field of transportation and communication generally which is vital to our development, and in the more settled areas of our country. We know what that has included. It has included the transcontinental television system, improved airports and facilities and construction of oil and gas pipe lines. However, the two great projects which perhaps were most characteristic of the bold action taken in this sector during that period were the trans-Canada highway and the St. Lawrence seaway, which is very much in our minds these days and to which the hon. member for Laurier made so great a contribution.
Our national development policy also provided special encouragement to the utilization and conservation of our resources. Extended geological surveys and the special three-year tax exemption period certainly 57071-3-124
National Development Policy contributed to increased mining operations in Canada. A most spectacular development in that field, one concerning which I have perhaps more knowledge than I have of some of the others, was the development of uranium mining brought about by carefully worked out policies between the producers, the federal government and the provincial governments concerned and also-this is most important- brought about because marketing arrangements were made, satisfactory to the producers, with the government of the United States, which was the only government at that time that could serve as a market for our uranium production. So successful, so spectacular, has that development been

and perhaps the most spectacular part of it is centred around the Elliot Lake-Blind River area-that if it were not for the increased exports of uranium to the United States in the current year our figures for exports to that country would not be nearly as high as they are today.
Then there was federal assistance to the provinces for forest inventories, reforestation and fire prevention, all of which led to a better knowledge of our forest resources and to more efficient measures for the conservation of those resources. Special legislation was introduced to make sure that water resources would be used in the best interests of Canada, and we know the increasing importance of that subject. A special program of assistance for the Atlantic provinces was inaugurated, which certainly comes within the field of national development. This involved coal subventions, mechanization programs, increased assistance under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, the construction of thermal power plants and interconnecting power lines, and the establishment of an interdepartmental committee to make recommendations on the integration and provision of transportation facilities.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, a new element altogether was added to our national development some years ago by assistance to housing and to municipalities. Under the National Housing Act and other legislation the former federal government participated in the construction of several hundreds of thousands of houses throughout Canada. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is an important phase of national development. Provision was also made under that legislation to pay 75 per cent of the cost of constructing low cost housing for rent, and there was federal participation in redevelopment projects and slum clearance programs.
This review-and it is a very cursory review omitting many things-shows that our post-war period of national development was vigorous and dynamic despite the special

National Development Policy circumstances of that period. Those special circumstances, which made the discharge of federal governmental responsibilities in national development not easy, were outlined by Mr. St. Laurent, prime minister at that time, in his opening remarks at the federal-provincial conference in October, 1955. Among other things he said:
In its own fields of responsibility the federal government has followed a vigorous policy of public investment since the end of the war, tempered, of course, by the overriding needs of defence in the past five years and also by the need for restraint because of the dangers of inflation and our desire to postpone what could reasonably be postponed so that it would not compete with a high level of private investment.
That was the situation which confronted us in those years when the government attempted to assist by public projects in national development, at a time when the great danger to the economy of the country was inflation, when it seemed undesirable for the government to interfere with private development except in so far as that interference was necessary to facilitate such private development.

What date was that, or
what page?

That was in October, 1955 and it is either on page 11 or page 12 of the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference of 1955. The national development policy of the new government was announced in the speech from the throne in October, 1957, but no indication was given then as to its general aims or content or the principles that underlie it. Specific references were made in that speech only to further assistance to power development in the Atlantic provinces, to the South Saskatchewan dam and to the negotiations initiated by the Liberal government with the United States on the question of Columbia river power development.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, nothing has been done as far as we know with respect to new thermal power developments in the Atlantic provinces apart from the signing of a master agreement. Certain Nova Scotia mines are temporarily, and we hope only temporarily, closed. No agreement has yet been reached on the South Saskatchewan dam, a project which we were led to hope would begin last autumn. No report has yet been made to the house on the negotiations with the United States respecting the Columbia river matter. Nor have we heard anything at all about the activities of the interdepartmental committee of officials on transportation in the Atlantic provinces which was set up by the previous government more than a year ago, and which we thought could do useful work

in those provinces in developing co-operation between the federal and provincial governments on transportation matters.
During the election campaign the Conservative party put particular emphasis on a so-called special public investment program to meet the recession, and we heard a good deal at that time about the vision of northern development. We contended at that time, and I think the Canadian people now realize, that the special public works program for unemployment relief amounting to over a billion dollars announced by the Prime Minister never in fact existed. In fact, government expenditures for this purpose in 1958-1959 will be roughly about the same level as they were in the previous years of so-called Liberal neglect and postponement. Of course new projects will be initiated in 1958-59, but there is nothing exceptional about this, especially if you take into account the fact that most of these projects were planned and prepared by the former government. Apart from the very limited action taken by the government in co-operation with the provinces with regard to access roads, we are left with vague pronouncements and a postelection works mirage.
Therefore it appears to us, Mr. Speaker, that the government record, especially viewed in the light of the perfervid words of the election campaign, has not yet been very impressive in this field. Certainly so far as the use of these methods for unemployment relief and for curing the recession is concerned the results have been very meagre indeed. But, Mr. Speaker, we are quite ready to wait and give the government a fair chance to show some creative imagination in the pursuit of this national policy. We are ready to help in this regard and make what we think are concrete, constructive and practical suggestions.
From igloo to igloo.
I will come to that also.
You had better crawl out.

I do not have to worry about that, and I will be able to convince my hon. friends without any difficulty.
Now, our only purpose in presenting today the amendment I am about to propose is to call the attention of the government to the need for a new development policy in line with the current economic and social requirements of the Canadian people. These current economic and social requirements have changed even over the last two years.
Up to now, Mr. Speaker, when we have attempted to make any constructive suggestions the government or a spokesman for the government, instead of discussing these

proposals on their own merits, usually has asked the question, sometimes jocularly and sometimes in a worse than jocular way, "Why did you not do it before?" Such a reaction, Mr. Speaker, is not very intelligent nor very serious. It will be more than usually unjustified during this debate because very important changes have occurred in the economic conditions governing the aims and content of our development policy in the last year or so.
These changes, which should be obvious to everyone, are the result of several factors, two of which I should like to mention. In the first place, Mr. St. Laurent asserted in the statement I quoted earlier that our post-war development of this country was tempered by our desire in those years to postpone what could be reasonably postponed so it would not compete with the high level of private investment, and we certainly had a high level of private investment during those years. That factor has disappeared since private investments, for the time being, are certainly declining. Government action now becomes necessary to fill the gap in a way which was not the case two, three or four years ago.
In the second place, some of the major projects in the public investment program initiated by the former government have been completed or will soon be completed. This is true, for instance, in the case of the construction of the seaway, the trans-Canada pipe line, the trans-Canada highway, and several airport and harbour improvements. Other major projects, therefore, must be planned and initiated if the level of public investment in Canada is to be maintained or increased. There is greater necessity for that at the present time than there has been at any time since world war II.
These factors, then, are changing the public investment picture in this country quite drastically at the present time. They call for a new orientation or a new emphasis in our national development policy if we want to maintain the kind of balance and dynamism which we have achieved in the past.
We on this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, feel as we did in the past, that the development of the far north above the 60th parallel is directly the responsibility of the federal government and would continue to be one very important aspect of the national policy. Government assistance to the population in the north is not only desirable but it is necessary.
I do not for one minute, however, accept the contention of Conservative spokesmen in the last election campaign that this kind of program in the Arctic about which they
57071-3-124J
National Development Policy talked at that time, a road program, a transportation program, would have any considerable effect, if any effect at all, in the immediate emergency which confronted us, which was unemployment. It is one thing to put forward a program for national development in the Arctic, but it is another thing to put forward a program of that kind, especially when it is contained in estimates which have already been drawn up, as a cure for the unemployment emergency.
This kind of claim during an election campaign or subsequent to an election campaign, and even if it is made in this house this afternoon, does not make sense. A program of national development in the north to improve transportation and communication for national development purposes, carrying on the planning and development which has been going on for years, does make sense.
There are a good many reasons now, Mr. Speaker, why government action is necessary in this respect in the north to a greater degree than it has been in recent years. In the first place, there is the growing number of companies already located in that region, and their workers, who are entitled to government services. These companies have not come in within the last 12 months. They have been coming in during recent years.
Moreover the local population, the Indians and Eskimos, is now increasing and it is more difficult for these aboriginal people, these earliest inhabitants of our country, to adapt themselves to new conditions. They see their traditional methods of livelihood disappearing. They see new activities coming into their country. They see the basis of their previous existence changing. There is, therefore, a special obligation on the government to help them adapt themselves to the new conditions for which we are largely responsible. This means the government will have to assist the native population to learn new trades and create for them new employment opportunities.
There are also political as well as military reasons which justify a continued emphasis on the development of the north. We are claiming, and rightly, our sovereignty over that portion of our territory. Indeed, we have claimed sovereignty under what we call the sector theory over the prolongation north, right to their meeting at the north pole, of the east and west extensions of our boundary. If we are to make that claim stick, and it certainly is important we should make it stick, we have to do everything that is possible, everything that is practical, to develop those areas and reinforce whatever rights we may have in law with the right of occupation.

National Development Policy
Then, finally, such development is justified because we will, in time, need the vast resources found in this area for our future prosperity and expansion. The Canadian north is now fairly well known for its abundant and diversified natural resources. Some of them are already being exploited. It must be recognized that the world demand for minerals of all kinds is rising steadily. On the other hand, lest our enthusiasm for Arctic development run away with us, we should remember also that a good many of these metals, under present conditions, are in surplus supply. I know that in the long run we have no reason to be pessimistic about the future of base metal production in this country. The Paley report-and we always quote the Paley report when we discuss a question of this kind-has shown that the mineral reserves of the United States are becoming depleted. For these reasons, and because the Canadian north is one of the last economic frontiers in the world, long-term prospects for its development are very bright indeed.
However, there are also very good reasons why we as a nation should not proceed too fast with the opening up of the Canadian north, why we should not speed up its development in disregard of economic conditions. Indeed, I am reminded that the minister of northern affairs himself, and I think he was quite sound in this statement, said the other day that it would be unwise for instance to bring a road through for a commodity before there was a market for that commodity.
There is a common fallacy about the impact that accelerated northern development could have at this time on the Canadian economy. It is often urged that this impact would be similar to that which resulted from the opening up of the west. Surely we would be unwise to try to carry that parallel too far. We should remind ourselves that wheat production was supplementary at that time, in opening up the west, to the industrial activity of eastern Canada. Mineral production in the far north at the present time, in most cases and for the time being, will be merely a supplement or an addition to what we have already in relative abundance in the northern portions of our provinces.
For some time to come, therefore, the mineral production of the north will not be complementary to but will be competitive with similar production of other Canadian regions on world markets. A very good example of that, of course, is the uranium mining industry itself. We have perhaps the largest single uranium field in the free world, at least, in the Elliot Lake-Blind River area, and there is a good deal more uranium up
[Mr, Pearson.1
there that has not yet been brought under production. It is accessible to the consuming centres in the United States. Indeed, the only consuming centre in the United States is the government of the United States. Therefore to spend energy and money at this time in trying to open up new sources of uranium say in the far north, when we have so much closer to home and closer to markets, would not, I believe, be an economic or wise proposition.
In order to be competitive with other sources of supply on world markets at the same price, most of this increased mineral production in the north would have to be subsidized in one form or another because of its relative geographical remoteness from world markets. The basic problem raised for us by accelerated economic development in the north at this stage-and I am sure the minister will agree with me in this-can be defined very simply. Production and transportation costs in that region are much higher than they are in other areas of our country and in other parts of the world. Yet products originating in the north must be sold on world markets at competitive prices.
I was reading the reports of the meeting of the Royal society in Edmonton which was held a few weeks ago. One of the papers, given by Mr. Legget of the national research council, pointed out that it cost as much to transport building material from Edmonton to Aklavik as to purchase the building material in Edmonton. In view of these circumstances, therefore-high transportation costs, the situation with regard to world markets, the fact that in some cases we are producing in surplus supply some of these materials in other parts of Canada-it would seem to me unwise, without most careful consideration of the economic problems involved, to rush into the development of the north at this stage through subsidized transportation, especially when the resulting increased production might depress production in other parts of Canada and therefore might interfere with the production with the wellbeing of those other parts of Canada.
As I see it, what we should do is not slow down on the planning and development which have been going on in recent years but carry that forward wherever economic consideration would justify it, to take the necessary action but to be very careful indeed in present conditions that economic circumstances justify the action before that action is taken. We do not have to worry about these resources; they are there, and they will be of great value to the world in the years ahead. Surely the thing to do now is to plan and develop for those years ahead

carefully and soundly and with all the vigour which is required by any particular policy.
I believe that we should continue to emphasize the importance of the north and treat it as I have suggested it should be treated in regard to economic development, moving vigorously but moving carefully. I think also that a very important part of national development policy remains in those other areas and those other sectors of the Canadian economy which have been the subject of governmental help and intervention over the years.
For instance, an extremely important aspect of national development is research itself. In 1956-57 the government spent $106 million on research. I suggest that we can do better than that. I suggest-and this suggestion has already been made officially by our party-that there should be set up a national science commission to promote, sponsor and co-ordinate scientific development and research in Canada upon whatever government level it may be conducted. I suggest also that a very important aspect of national development is assistance by the federal government to the provinces so they may be in a position to develop their own resources to the maximum possible extent.
I am thinking particularly at the moment of communications and transportation. I am thinking of the proposal which our party has already made that the federal government should become responsible for 95 per cent of the cost of the remaining parts of the trans-Canada highway in the four Atlantic provinces. I am thinking of the assistance that we have proposed should be given to those provinces for trunk highways which would increase communication between the Atlantic provinces and other parts of Canada and the United States. I am also thinking of a railway to Great Slave lake which is now very much under consideration, I know, by the government. I am also thinking of the building with federal assistance of a second trans-Canada highway through Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Edmonton, and the Peace river district to the Pacific.
I am also thinking-and perhaps there is no more important aspect of national development where the federal government can be more immediately helpful-of assistance to the municipalities in the problems that face them, which are a part of national development because national development is the sum of local development. What more important form could national development at this time take than federal assistance to the municipalities in slum clearance and
National Development Policy urban redevelopment projects? We therefore propose greater federal participation in such projects. Raising the proposed federal share to 50 per cent or 75 per cent of the cost of slum clearance projects would be justified on the grounds of national development.
I should like to put forward another proposal which is part of our party platform. I am very happy to mention these party proposals which we put forward in the election campaign, and to put them on Hansard as something we think should be done, not merely to be put forward for election purposes but put forward after the election is over as something that we think is constructive. For that purpose I suggest to the government they should consider the establishment at this time-and they are going to have a municipal-provincial-federal conference one of these days or one of these months or one of these years-of a municipal loan fund by which capital could be made available to the municipalities on a longterm basis for major municipal improvements, for the expansion of urgently needed municipal services.
Did my hon. friends not turn that down when they were in power?

I do not think it was ever turned down when we were in power. But what difference does that make? Every time we make a proposal over here in the opposition somebody on the other side, instead of examining the proposal and seeing whether it fits the situation, immediately says, "You didn't do it in 1935" or "You didn't do it in 1945". I suggest to the Prime Minister that he look ahead occasionally and not keep looking back into the record of the past.
Oh, oh.

If he will look ahead and consider these problems that the municipalities face-and we hear a good deal about them these days-perhaps he will find something worthy of support in the establishment of a municipal loan fund for the purposes I have indicated. The scope and administrative set-up of that fund would, of course, have to be settled in consultation with representatives of the provinces and municipalities, but it is something which my hon. friend might well take up with the provinces and municipalities when he next meets them. If they could work out something like that we, of course, would be glad to give him and his government all the credit for it.
Within limits.

Within limits, as my friend the hon. member for Essex East cautions.

National Development Policy
Repentance is good for the soul.

There is one other proposal that I should like to make. This also is one that we have put forward more than once, one also that we were not in a position to implement over the years when we were in power, and it also has a very special relationship to the circumstances of today, which in this regard are much different from what they were five or ten years ago. That is the establishment of a national advisory board on economic development and automation for dealing with long term problems of production and employment. We suggest that such an advisory board be established, staffed by representatives from labour, industry, agriculture and the universities as well as government. One principal duty of such a board would be to study the long term measures required to ensure a high level of employment and to minimize for workers the consequences of automation by providing for re-training programs, better mobility of workers and other progressive measures.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Could he explain the difference between this proposed board and the Gordon commission?

This board, in the terms in which I am putting it forward was not, so far as my recollection goes, recommended by the Gordon commission at all. I do not think the Gordon commission report had anything to say with regard to it in terms of a recommendation to deal with it-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member has misunderstood me. Will he explain the difference between the commission he is now recommending and the commission which his government set up known as the Gordon commission.

I find it easy to do that. The Gordon commission was a commission set up by the government to investigate and report, and as a result of its report on general economic conditions, as a result of its general economic survey of the country it was hoped that whatever government might be in power at the time the report was received would find recommendations which would be useful if embodied in the permanent machinery of government. I am suggesting that this proposal is very different indeed, that this commission should become an agency of the government to consider the problems I have mentioned and one or two which I should like to mention. The Gordon commission was a fact finding body set up to report to the government. We are suggesting to the government now


that they should set up a piece of government machinery which would, I think, be of a constructive and useful nature.
Among other things, the duty of this board would be to plan programs for long term development which would ensure the steady progress of the Canadian economy and help to sustain full employment.
How far would its powers go?

I am making this recommendation to the government. The government will undoubtedly desire to look into it and consider how far its powers should extend. Its powers would have to be circumscribed in the legislation setting up the board. I do not think the Prime Minister would wish me to go further into the matter at this time, but I throw the suggestion out to him and to the government since they have to face not only the immediate problems of recession and unemployment but also the longer range problems of economic planning and development which in the long run may be even more important.
I think I have said enough to show that national development covers a great many subjects, and that while national development in the north is important, national development in other parts of Canada is equally important. There is much to be done, and I suggest to the Prime Minister that while it is of first and immediate importance to deal with the problems immediately before us, the recession and unemployment, it is of almost equal importance in the long run, if not even more important, to look ahead and plan to deal with the problems that will be facing us in the future. It is in that spirit that I put forward these suggestions. Because we on this side of the house do not feel that the government is tackling these problems of national development with the constructive energy and purpose which we think to be desirable in the present circumstances, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "That" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that, in present circumstances of declining private investment, a balanced policy of national development requires consideration by the government of active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital especially in the form of transportation facilities, municipal improvements, and other facilities to stimulate economic development and to promote social wellbeing in the settled areas of Canada."

Mr. Speaker, I must say that we in this group have listened with the greatest interest and delight to the words uttered by the Leader

of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in the very good speech he has just made.
When we hear the leader of the Liberal opposition using such words as "economic planning and development" and stressing the need for social capital in the amendment he moves, and in the remarks he made during his speech; and when he suggests, as he obviously does, that in order to rescue this country from the deficiencies of private enterprise we should use the national credit, then I can only say that I have sent to my office for an application form to be sent to the Leader of the Opposition in order to give him the opportunity of joining the C.C.F.
As I say, we were delighted and amazed. Only time will tell whether these are just words, or whether they are words that will be followed by action. But we were delighted to hear this point of view put forward and we support many of the suggestions he made with respect to the need for a national development policy, the need for social capital and the need for economic planning. It pleases us very much to realize that this small group at this end of the house is so effective in its presentation of the policy and program of the C.C.F. that it has now succeeded, in the short time of slightly more than two months, in inoculating the hon. gentlemen on our physical left-whether they are on our ideological left will only be determined after the passage of time.
However that may be, Mr. Speaker, I must say that we have repeatedly in this house urged many of these things which have been advocated by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, and we shall continue to do so. We realize that if we are going to have a balanced national development we must have economic planning as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition. We need, also, the social capital mentioned in the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition, and we have always preached the necessity for the use of the national credit to this end.
A national development program from our point of view would require participation by the federal government, by the provincial governments and by the municipal governments. We think that a balanced national development program would include the building of large hydro projects. When such projects are mentioned we, in British Columbia, immediately think of the development of the Columbia river and its hydro resources.
We think of the necessity of a greatly expanded national highways program in this country, of the necessity of a second trans-Canada highway, of the need for a national conservation policy, the necessity of greatly extended assistance through some type of fund perhaps as suggested by the leader of
National Development Policy the official opposition to the municipalities and of the necessity for taking advantage of opportunities to put to work idle Canadians in the development of our national parks and recreational facilities. But in addition to these things we in the C.C.F. believe we should also utilize the national credit for the assistance of small business in Canada because we realize that small business is a very important part of the economy of this country.
Other hon. members in this group who will follow me as this debate proceeds today and tomorrow will deal with other aspects of this problem-the federal, provincial and municipal aspects-and will possibly deal with some of the details which I have previously skirted but it is my intention in the brief time I will detain the house to deal solely with the need for social capital being used in the development of small business or small free enterprise in Canada.
Quite recently, I believe, I mentioned that the philosophy of the policy and program of the C.C.F. recognizes the importance of the small business sector of our economy as part of a mixed economy. I judge from the smiles on the faces of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the leader of the official opposition that they are somewhat under the delusion that all our policies are becoming mixed during this debate but what I am suggesting today has been the policy of the C.C.F. for a considerable length of time. That is to say, we believe in the great opportunity for social planning and the use of national credit in public ownership in the federal, provincial and municipal fields in a mixed economy, and the great opportunity for the development of the co-operative movement in this country whether it is in the form of a service cooperative, a consumer co-operative or a credit co-operative. In addition to that we believe in the great opportunity for the expansion of what we term as legitimate free enterprise where the real and genuine element of competition enters for the protection of the Canadian consumer. There is a great opportunity for the development of free enterprise in small industry, in distribution, retail outlets, and things of that type and in certain transportation and services generally.
Small business, generally speaking, is usually a community enterprise. It is established in its initial stages by local capital and employs local labour. Consequently there is an interest on the part of these local citizens of the community and a sense of responsibility on the part of the small business to the local community in which it operates. It participates in community activities, development, affairs and administration and differs somewhat from foreign capital or large scale investment in a significant way. In most

National Development Policy cases the profits made by a small business or free enterprise undertaking remain in the local community and are normally re-invested there so there is no net loss in profits to the community by their being exported to a country other than Canada. With the development of our country grows the opportunity and the need for a greater expansion of what we in this group call the legitimate free enterprise sector of our economy and that is the point I intend to deal with briefly this afternoon.
The bugbear, shall I say, or the major problem of small business, particularly in recent years where rapid expansion occurs and requirements have to be met fairly rapidly in our modern industrial society, is that there is a lack of long term credit. As hon. members know bank credit is too short to frequently satisfactorily serve the long term needs of small business and small industry. In that respect I want to speak from my personal experience and when I say that I refer to observations I have made in the district in which I have had the good fortune to live for over 50 years. I realize from what I have seen there that over and over again the efforts of hardworking, capable people have been frustrated and there has been a great deal of effort lost and wasted because they lacked the advantage of long term low interest capital to carry on their small business or industry.
I refer particularly to two aspects of small industry for which there is a major place in the economy of the district in which I live and in the general economy of British Columbia, and that is the need for and the value of small industry in the logging, sawmill and lumber processing industries. Regardless of the efficiency of large companies and the capital they can accumulate there are certain types of timber, certain locations and certain areas that can only be-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I take it he is leading up to a further amendment because his discourse is not on the subject that is now before the house?
Mr. Speaker, I am dealing with one aspect of the need for social capital.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I fail to see how this dissertation on long term credit for small business comes under the heading of social capital, in the words of the amendment:
-especially in the form of transportation facilities municipal improvements, and other facilities to stimulate economic development and to promote social well-being in the settled areas of Canada.
If the hon. member is leading up to an amendment I will not object, but if he is

speaking to the amendment now before the house, I consider him out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I was leading up to an amendment and you pushed me right in the door. At this point I shall move my amendment so as to bring myself in order. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That the amendment be further amended by inserting therein after the words "in the form of" the following words:
"long term loans to qualifying small businesses,"

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will put the motion when the hon. member completes his remarks.

Having now regularized the proceedings and having once again received your beneficent glances, Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate that the amendment as amended would now read:
That all the words after the word "That" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that, in present circumstances of declining private investment, a balanced policy of national development requires consideration by the government of active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital especially in the form of long term loans to qualifying small businesses, transportation facilities, municipal improvements, and other facilities to stimulate economic development and to promote social well-being in the settled areas of Canada.
Before placing my amendment, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with my personal experience with respect to the need for long term low interest capital for small industry and small business. I was dealing particularly with the need for it in small logging and sawmill enterprises. I mentioned the importance and necessity of maintaining these small enterprises in the forest industry particularly because of their social value and significance and because there is no other form of organized economic activity-except where it is possible to utilize a small co-operative organization-that can harvest this timber under certain circumstances and manufacture it to the mutual advantage of the state and those operating the industry.
I have known a number of men who have had the ability, the necessary small mill, the available timber and the market and yet they have failed for one reason only and that was the lack of adequate long term low interest capital. In the circumstances in which they were able to borrow capital there was not sufficient time for them to continue to operate and reinvest any surplus they might make in the industry which they were operating. It is therefore necessary in these circumstances, particularly in the forest industry-and I am dealing with an industry of which I know a little-because capital has to be invested in roads, in decking logs in the winter and so on. Under certain

conditions logs cannot be towed or trucked out until spring, or lumber has to be piled up over a period of months in order for it to dry before it can be sold. Therefore, inevitably a relatively large amount of investment is required, over which the operator himself has little control. Therefore, he requires this long term low interest capital in order to satisfactorily function and have an opportunity to get on his feet.
As I said before, I use those two illustrations in particular because over a period of 50 years I have seen so many capable, hardworking men finally lose what they had invested over a long period of years because they had insufficient capital to carry on until a surplus could be accumulated. This problem affects the small businessman across Canada in whatever type of business he may be, and it affects the small farmer for the same reasons I have outlined.
This group has given considerable study to this problem as a result of its experience and its observations and as a result of consultation with people who have done a considerable amount of research on the problem along monetary lines and discussions with the people directly concerned. For years I have been of the opinion, as have other members of this group, that one of the things that is sadly required is an opportunity for long term low interest capital.
About a week ago the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) spoke on this problem, presented our proposals and gave some details in that respect. I am not going to deal with that aspect of the situation this afternoon. I simply outline our general approach to it, our firm belief that small business is an essential part of the mixed economy which we as democratic socialists believe is the next step in the economic evolution of our society. For that reason we are particularly pleased to support the proposals made in the amendment by the Leader of the Opposition, and in order to complete the picture, in order to provide what we would term a truly balanced economy, we have amended the amendment in the way I have just placed before the house. That is all I have to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, and as I said before other hon. members will deal with other aspects of this problem from our point of view during this debate.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

In the hon. member's
opinion, when does a qualifying small business, which he mentioned in his subamendment, become a big business and no longer qualify?
57071-3-125
National Development Policy

I think the border line would be this. A large business is able to accumulate capital by the issuance of shares on the market and bonds and debentures, and things of that kind. The type of business that we speak of has no access to that capital in the same way because of its local and personal management and the lack of general knowledge by the public concerning the operation of the business in question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the amendment which he proposed, as well as to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), who has moved a subamendment. I should like to tell him at once that I find myself in sympathy with the proposal he has made and I would also like to tell him that because of his solicitude for small business I think I will send him an application to join the Liberal party.
We on this side of the house have always felt that particular attention should be given to small business. We have advocated that-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Since you got over there.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -down through the years and over the long term of years that we were in office-

You
did nothing about it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-we paid particular attention to that sector of the economy. For that reason, I think we will have no difficulty in supporting the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
I now turn my attention to the amendment moved by my leader and in order not to read it I summarize it by saying that it seeks a balanced policy of national development, requiring active measures to meet present-day needs in the form of transportation facilities. While it goes much farther than that, it is to that aspect of the amendment that I should like to direct my attention, namely that part which has to do with transportation facilities. Such a policy of national development did exist when the former Liberal government was in office. Indeed my leader dealt with the three periods since confederation and paid particular attention to that period which followed the war. In the field of transportation alone the policy which was advocated by the previous administration was not only a dynamic one but it was a forwardlooking one.
All one has to do in order to come to that conclusion is to look at the measures that were placed on the statute books of parliament. As a matter of fact, in the short time
1970	HOUSE OF
National Development Policy that I was in the Department of Transport as its head there were a large number of such measures that were advocated, put into effect and now are in operation in this country. I think of the construction of the various railway branch lines across this country; I think of the branch lines from Terrace to Kitimat, from Sherridon to Lynn Lake, from Barraute to Kiask Falls in the province of Quebec, and later from Kiask Falls to Beatty-ville, and later from Beattyville to Chibou-gamau and now under construction, by virtue of legislation passed in those years, the line from Chibougamau to the lake St. John area. The Canso causeway was a project that took a considerable time to put into effect but, following surveys which were made, action was taken upon it and that causeway has now been completed. Then there is the Canadian National Railways hotel and the aviation building in Montreal; airport development from one end of this country to the other, from Gander, following the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, right out to the west coast; harbour improvements in the national harbours of this country; the Prince Edward Island car ferry; the studies into the construction of a causeway from the mainland to Prince Edward Island, which are being followed by the present government and which have been mentioned on more than one occasion by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and others during the past few months.
There are also the new car ferry from North Sydney to Newfoundland, the terminal facilities at Port aux Basques and North Sydney, the construction of the Bluenose to operate a service between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor, the construction of new icebreakers for service on the St. Lawrence and elsewhere in the gulf and studies leading to the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake.
Here I should like to reiterate a point made by the Leader of the Opposition. In a brief submitted to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by R. G. Robertson, commissioner of the Northwest Territories and deputy minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, he advocates the following at page 24 thereof:
May I submit for the consideration of the commission three methods by which transportation facilities into the Northwest Territories might be improved. The first is the construction of a railroad to Great Slave lake. The second is construction of roads into promising resource development areas when and as indications suggest that these areas, given highway transportation, would be economic to develop. The third is the adoption of the policy of supplying the newly constructed defence stations in the Northwest Territories by commercial air services and the establishment of a network of scheduled commercial air lines in the Arctic.
[Mr. Chevrier.l

I compare this with a paragraph in the speech from the throne reading as follows:
In order to promote our national development on the frontier in the north you will be asked to authorize the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. My ministers regard this as a major step in the establishment of productive industry on an economic basis in the Northwest Territories. You will also be asked to provide for the construction of important roads needed for development in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and in the provinces, with the co-operation of their governments.
The brief to the Gordon commission is dated November 27, 1955, and unquestionably was the basis for the action which the government now proposes to take as outlined in the speech from the throne read in the other place on May 12. There is no question, but that many of the projects which were outlined and begun under the former Liberal administration are being continued now. I can understand how it is that in the time our friends were in office following the election of June 10, 1957 there was not much time for planning. In fact, there has been little time for planning because we have either been in session or in the midst of an election campaign, and if one believes the statements made in the house and outside by members of the government that the last session of parliament was nothing more or less than preparation for the election which took place on March 31 it then becomes quite clear and logical that there was no time for planning. Therefore our friends on the other side of the house have had to have recourse to a number of projects which were in the course of preparation by the previous administration.
I could go on and talk about other projects such as the trans-Canada highway but I have reason to speak particularly today about a great project, about a project which to my mind represents the greatest project that has ever been undertaken by two nations. I refer to the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway.
No one has done more for that than you have.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is the greatest international project ever launched by two nations.
What did you leave it for?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I gave the reasons before why I left and I am not the slightest bit sorry that I left in view of the fact that many public servants, one after the other, are leaving the service of the government of Canada.
I am glad you are not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
However, I rose to speak on the St. Lawrence seaway for two reasons. First, I wish to indicate that, in my opinion, no other project comparable to it has been brought forward by our friends on the other

side of the house, and I am sure there will not be one comparable to it for some time to come. The other reason I rose was to take issue with some of the statements that have been made recently by certain individuals in connection with it.
The St. Lawrence seaway is a power and navigation project. It consists of a 27-foot channel extending from the port of Montreal to lake Erie. It also consists of the joint development by Canada and the United States through their respective agencies of 2,200,000 horsepower of electrical energy in the international rapids section of the river. During four days of last week we witnessed the ceremonies which took place at Cornwall to mark the blowing up of the cofferdam and the creation of an artificial lake or pool above the dam indicating the beginning of gradual power development in that area. We witnessed the changeover of 14-foot navigation from the Canadian side to the United States side. Twenty-seven foot facilities will not be ready until the opening of navigation in 1959.
I should like to pause for a moment to pay tribute to certain individuals who had a great deal to do with the construction of the project. I should like to pay particular tribute to the officers and men of the hydroelectric power commission of the province of Ontario. I do not think any men contributed more towards the successful construction of the power aspect of this scheme than did the officials of Ontario hydro. They are, of course, extremely competent. In the Niagara peninsula area and on the Ottawa river they have built power projects of tremendous importance and I can do nothing else than to pay to these men who built the facilities in the international section in conjunction with the St. Lawrence seaway authority the tribute of competence and understanding.
I should like to single out the late Bob Saunders, a former president of Ontario hydro, who had a great deal to do with the negotiations leading to the agreement between the province of Ontario and Canada. I should also like to mention the name of Dr. Otto Holden, chief engineer of Ontario hydro, who in part designed many of the structures which went into this development. Last but not least there is that kind, understanding, able and competent project engineer stationed at Cornwall, Gordon Mitchell, who did a tremendous amount for the success of this enterprise.
I have nothing but commendation for the manner in which the officials of Ontario hydro built the plant. If I had a complaint it would be that it seems to me that Ontario 57071-3-1251
National Development Policy hydro should have given consideration to setting aside a block of power for development of industry in the eastern Ontario region. The New York state power authority on the United States side gave consideration to that aspect of the question and set aside blocks of power so that today there are two large industries located just east of Massena along the south shore of the St. Lawrence river opposite the city of Cornwall.
One is Reynolds Aluminum, a large industry, and another is an automobile manufacturing plant, both of which came there because of the inducement they had in regard to these blocks of power set aside by the New York state commission for that purpose. It seems to me that Ontario hydro, instead of feeding all of this power into the grid for the development of the metropolitan areas of Toronto and Hamilton and the southern Ontario peninsula, might well have given consideration to the setting aside of a block of power for the development of industry in eastern Ontario.
I would not like to leave the question of the construction of this project without recalling to the house the name of another great public servant who had a great deal to do with the St. Lawrence seaway and who, in my estimation, is probably the man who knows more about the project than anyone else in this country, a man who, I am sure, has contributed tremendously to the negotiations as well as the preparations for the navigation aspects of the project. I refer to Mr. R. A. C. Henry, a consulting engineer now in the city of Montreal. The government of Canada appointed him as head of the special projects branch of the Department of Transport. He was a man with a great deal of experience; a former deputy minister of railways and canals; a former deputy minister of the department of reconstruction. He was responsible, in large part, for the setting up of the department of reconstruction and supply, following the war years, and he became chairman of the air transport board. Few men, I say, are as well informed or as conversant as he is with all aspects of both power and navigation. I could not rise at this time without making some reference to the tremendous contribution made by Mr. R. A. C. Henry, not only to the economic development of Canada but to transportation development in Canada generally and more particularly to the St. Lawrence seaway project.
There are other aspects of this problem to which I should like to refer. In making these references, I should like to stress the magnitude of this enterprise. I said at the outset that I did not believe there was any

National Development Policy project that compared in magnitude. I said that because it is not only a great engineering project, but you have dams that were built across streams; you have power structures that were built on the bed of the river; you have islands that were excavated and dredged in order to make way for the navigation channel; and in some areas you have the level of the water being raised 50 feet above the present level. The seaway is not only a great engineering project, but it is a great social achievement. It is a great social achievement because whole communities were wiped out by the formation of this lake in the last few days, and in their stead modern communities have arisen on the new shoreline. Parks and parkways have been built for recreational purposes on both sides of the line.
The seaway is first and foremost however, a great international project. It is one thing for two governments to get together and decide upon the construction of an international project, but it is another thing for that project to be put into effect. There are groups on a lower level than that of government who must co-operate in order to bring about the successful accomplishment of a project such as this. In this case there were no less than four international bodies composed of Canadians and United States representatives who had to work hand in hand in solving the problems that confronted us. There is the St. Lawrence river joint board of engineers, which approved of the plans and specifications and which supervises the work during construction. There is the international St. Lawrence river board of control whose duties relate to the water levels and regulate what the discharge of water will be from lake Ontario and the flow of water through the international rapids section. There is the international lake Ontario board of engineers which recommended a plan of regulation for the water level in the international section, and which today the government accepts. Finally, there is the international joint commission on whom the obligation is laid by the governments of Canada and the United States for the approval of the project. This body gave approval to the project and it keeps today a watchful eye over it.
It goes without saying that the parliament of Canada and the congress of the United States are the supreme authorities on this international project. Their will has been expressed by the designation of an entity to construct the power phases of the seaway in the international section. By agreement with the province of Ontario-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, may I suggest to your honour that the line the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) is now following has nothing to do with the amendment?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I be heard on the point of order? The amendment, and I hesitate to read it because it is of some length, reads:
That all the words after the word "That" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that, in present circumstances of declining private investment, a balanced policy of national development requires consideration by the government of active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital especially in the form of transportation facilities-
I will not go on any farther. I stop there because I am now discussing one of the greatest transportation projects, the St. Lawrence seaway. I want to talk about some of its effects, and to take issue with some of the statements that were made recently in connection with it. I am now laying the foundation of that, and this certainly has to do with a national development program, namely the amendment which you have had an opportunity of reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I point out that the hon. member was not dealing with transportation, he was dealing with the development of power between Ontario and the state of New York. I suggest that has nothing whatever to do with the amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: After reading carefully the amendment which is before me, I do not believe this amendment permits a discussion of one specific venture, and especially a venture which has already been partially realized. This amendment deals with measures which it is suggested the government should take to meet the urgent needs of social capital, especially in the form of transportation facilities, et cetera. I do not believe the hon. member for Laurier is actually covering the point in his comments about the St. Lawrence seaway. I would suggest he keep his remarks more in the form of suggestions to the government concerning action in the future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What I was trying to do was to show the magnitude of this project which, I assure you, is far from completion. There is a tremendous amount yet to be done before it can be completed. In fact, it will not be completed until the opening of navigation in 1959 and I doubt whether the full facilities will be completed then. But if my hon. friend feels that I am not in order in dealing with the power facilities-although I think that I am in order because they are still not completed-then I will relate my remarks to the navigational aspects of the seaway.

Here I should like to draw your attention to some of the facts of this project from a navigational standpoint. The advantages that will derive from this project from a navigational standpoint are widely dispersed and will be felt in the whole of the Canadian economy. There will be great economies and savings of no less than $48 million per year in transportation costs. This has been estimated to mean a reduction of anywhere from three cents to five cents per bushel in the cost of transportation thereon. I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), in announcing the tolls the other day, made some reference to that matter. This project will add not less than $100 million per year to the national income. It will increase total volume of traffic from 10 million to 35 million tons on the St. Lawrence. It will, it is estimated, bring down the St. Lawrence route no less than 200 million bushels of United States wheat. This is an advantage that had not been envisaged when the seaway was in the course of preparation. The statement which I have just made-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I again rise on a point of order. The hon. member is completely ignoring the ruling made by Your Honour just a few moments ago. He is going on to discuss the St. Lawrence seaway project at great length. If it is in order for him to do that, it would be just as much in order for him to discuss the construction of the C.P.R. across Canada-

Of course it
would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -or any other project that has been done in the past. I suggest that the hon. member must comply with Your Honour's ruling.
I wonder whether I might be permitted to say a word on the point of order?
Oh, oh.

Surely the leader of the government, in his new role as an exponent of the restriction of debate, would still not go as far as to suggest that in order to urge, as the hon. member has been doing, that projects of great importance for the improvement of transportation are necessary for the future, he could not illustrate them even by reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway, much less something that is far from being completed and about which the hon. gentleman has indicated he has some suggestions to make.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must remind hon. members that the amendment reads as follows:
National Development Policy
-a balanced policy of national development requires consideration by the government of active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital-

If I may do so I
should like to suggest to Your Honour, with great deference, that the terms of the resolution permit a wide latitude of discussion not envisaged in the restricted words which Your Honour has just used. I make that suggestion not in direct disagreement with what you have said but by way of seeking to bring Your Honour to a better understanding of the privileges of the house in respect of a resolution in these large and generous terms. In order to do that, I think one should read the full resolution, something which Your Honour did not do. The full resolution reads as follows:
That all the words after the word "That" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that, in present circumstances of declining private investment, a balanced policy of national development requires consideration by the government or active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital-
And these are the essential words which are at the basis of the right which we on this side of the house say the hon. gentleman has to discuss this matter.
-especially in the form of transportation facilities, municipal improvements, and other facilities-
I would ask you to note the words "other facilities".
-to stimulate economic development and to promote social well-being in the settled areas of Canada.
In other words, for the purpose of this argument the important word is "especially".
