The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) is discussing perhaps one of the most important projects ever conceived of by the government and the people of Canada. It is a scheme that is not complete, and one that

National Development Policy is still capable of meeting the urgent needs of social capital especially in the form of transportation facilities.
I would suggest that in taking the position which he has taken the leader of the house ought to bear in mind that the Speaker, for whom we have the greatest of respect and whose intentions we all recognize as being in the common interests of our deliberations, nevertheless is one who has not had the long experience of the Leader of the Opposition and others in this house in trying to ascertain the traditional freedom that is afforded to hon. members on a resolution of this kind. I think it is particularly true in the case of my friend the genial Leader of the Opposition-
The leader of the house.

-or rather the leader of the house for whom we all have the greatest respect. I was thinking of my friend a few years from now when I referred to him as the leader of the opposition. My hon. friend objected the other day to the hon. member for Laurier discussing this very question on his own estimates. In the light of that fact and in the light of words of conciliation which I have used, I would hope that we will be allowed to go on unfettered in this discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On the point of order may I say this, Mr. Speaker. As usual, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is very persuasive. However, may I point out to Your Honour that this is not a debate on the St. Lawrence seaway project. If the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) is allowed to go on and make the kind of speech he has been making, then any other member of this house is entitled to get to his feet and answer him about the St. Lawrence seaway project.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly he is. Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In fact, one hon. member has already asked me about rising to point out the mistakes that the hon. member for Laurier is making.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wish he would do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It only shows all too clearly how far out of order the hon. member is in trying to turn this debate into a debate on the St. Lawrence seaway project.
The leader of the house is apparently afraid that this might degenerate into a debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The debate must be confined to the wording of the amendment which was drawn up by my hon. friends opposite over


the week end. I do not doubt that they burned the midnight oil in working out this form of amendment.
We always work.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
However, now that they have submitted it, they are bound by it and they must keep to the terms of the amendment itself. As a matter of fact, there is one portion of the amendment itself which is out of order, namely that portion which refers to municipal improvements.
I refer Your Honour to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) during the debate on the address, which reads:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the advisability of passing legislation at this session to relieve the very heavy financial burden now carried by the municipalities of this country.
That, of course, is another point of order. But I would repeat that the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) had no right to turn this debate into a debate on the St. Lawrence seaway.

On this point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think that since the amendment is couched in very general terms it is one which enables the house to engage in a very wide ranging debate. That, of course, is perfectly proper and it is not necessary for hon. members when they engage in the discussion to stick to the wording of the resolution; they can bring forward examples to emphasize why they think the terms of the resolution should be adopted. And from our experience in this house on previous occasions I should think that any amendment which is moved asking that active measures should be taken to make available social capital in connection with transportation and other facilities would cover discussion of the St. Lawrence seaway project. Should other hon. members wish to reply to the hon. member for Laurier, I think they would be perfectly in order. Should any hon. member wish to make a reference, say, to Trans-Canada Air Lines as another example of transportation facilities which should be extended and increased, I believe he would be in order, though I am not thinking of doing so myself. It would seem to me, however, that a detailed review of what has gone on in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway in the past is not covered by this-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what he has been doing.

I do not think, however, that the leader of the house raised this as his point. My understanding is that he went a good deal further and said the St. Lawrence seaway could not be discussed under this

item at all. I think the seaway can be discussed to the extent that it is an active project today and to the extent that it may be increased and expanded as an active project in the future. As to a historical review of the project in the past, however-
That is what we have been getting.

-I think the leader of the house has a point. But surely projects such as the St. Lawrence seaway and the extension of the seaway, and the extension of other transportation facilities are precisely what this resolution is about.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That makes quite a number of points of order to deal with at one time. The amendment itself clearly states this:
-a balanced policy of national development requires consideration by the government of active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital especially in the form of transportation facilities, municipal improvements, and other facilities to stimulate economic development and to promote social well-being in the settled areas of Canada.
I believe transportation facilities may be discussed in relation to the urgent needs of social capital such as the amendment mentions, but I believe it is out of order at present to start a debate uniquely on the St. Lawrence seaway, and that it is out of order to review all that has happened in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway unless it is in relation to the suggestion relevant to the urgent needs of social capital mentioned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you made the point a moment ago that you thought I should not direct my remarks to what has been done but rather to what is being done, and that is what I am trying to do. I am trying to relate my remarks to what is being done; to relate them not so much to the past as to the present and to the future in relation to the urgent needs of social capital and in relation, also, to transportation needs. In that respect I was discussing the benefits that would derive from the seaway.
However, if you feel I should not dwell on that, I will pass to another part of my remarks which I think is pertinent to the amendment now before the house. The point I wanted to make is that although there has been a large amount of capital expenditure on the St. Lawrence seaway, because of what has happened from one end of it to the other there has now been more money spent for industrial development between the eastern end and the head of the great lakes than on the seaway itself. I am informed-and I relate this to the amendment-that the expenditure of large sums is being planned with respect to
National Development Policy capital development, and that large sums of money have already been, in a large part, spent for industrial development on the south shore in the Montreal area, in the Niagara peninsula and in other regions of the seaway from its eastern extremity to the head of the lakes.
The second purpose I had in rising was to take issue with a certain statement which was made recently on the subject by the premier of the province of Ontario.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house a report which appeared in the Cornwall Standard Freeholder of July 2, 1958, as follows:
Premier Leslie Frost has sounded a "battle cry" for an all-Canadian seaway.
Immediate indication is that he intends cashing in on Prime Minister Diefenbaker's "works program for Canada."
The premier of Ontario is reported as having said:
Ontario hydro has built the first part of an all Canadian seaway with construction of the $14,000,000 closure structure at the powerhouse.
The report continues:
Mr. Frost is actually picking up the reins from Hon. Lionel Chevrier, former member of parliament for Stormont and once president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, who fought for an all-Canadian seaway.
And then the premier is reported as saying that the time had come for the construction of an all-Canadian seaway, and that he supports that project. Now, I should like to say a word in connection with that, and to state that as far back as 1951-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I again rise on a point of order. Here we come back to the same old subject. The hon. gentleman is going back to rake over the coals in connection with this St. Lawrence seaway project, and I suggest that is not in order in this debate.

Surely the leader of the house is carrying things to an extreme. What the hon. member for Laurier had begun to do was to talk about a new project, the creation of an all-Canadian seaway which is not part of the scheme at present under contemplation, and surely that comes completely within the purview of this resolution; and, surely, it is impossible to start with tomorrow. One has to give some background to a project of this kind, as hon. members will discover when they start planning.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I suggest that the hon. member for Laurier is just trying to carry on an argument with the premier of Ontario here in this house on the particular amendment that is now before us.

Surely it is against the rules to impute motives.
1976	HOUSE OF
National Development Policy

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I was going on to say, if I may, that the premier in his statement in Cornwall advocated the construction of an all-Canadian seaway. What I wanted to bring to the attention of the house was that the previous government, as far back as 1951, had laid the foundation for the construction of an all-Canadian seaway; in fact, the cabinet approved the so-called all-Canadian seaway project in 1951, and at that time it was arranged that the then prime minister of Canada would discuss the project as it was then envisaged with the then president of the United States.
In the first place, when Canada saw that it was not possible to proceed with the 1941 agreement that had been signed by the two countries, another attitude was taken by this country, that of using the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act. Prior to making an application by both Canada and the United States for the development of power in the international section, Canada agreed to provide all of the navigational facilities on its side of the boundary line. It was then that the then prime minister went to discuss the matter with the president of the United States who agreed, that if congress did not give its approval to the 1941 agreement he would approve of the all-Canadian seaway as second best.
It was decided, however, that parliament should introduce legislation providing for the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act and providing also, by agreement between Ontario and Canada, for the development of power. Later on, in 1954, congress passed what is known as the Wiley Dondero act. That act instructed a United States entity to build all of the facilities in the international section on the United States side of the line and so, at that time, we had two statutes. We had the Canadian statute authorizing construction wholly within Canada and in conjunction with a United States authority alternatively and a United States statute authorizing construction of a project on the United States side. Therefore it became important that the two governments meet which they did in July of 1954 when it was agreed that Canada would build the Canadian facilities at Iroquois and the United States would build in the international section opposite Barnhart island with the distinct understanding that as and when the volume of traffic warranted Canada would build the Canadian facilities.
The point I wish to make now is that perhaps the premier of the province of Ontario did not think of it at the time, but there is today the Iroquois canal which is built exclusively on Canadian territory. There
I Mr. Pickersgill.]

is also the structure of the dike built at a cost of $14 million and pursuant to the agreement between Canada and Ontario by Ontario hydro and which provides for 27-foot facilities in the future. There is also the construction of channel facilities leading up to two Canadian locks opposite the city of Cornwall. As the matter now stands approximately half of the all-Canadian seaway is completed. All that remains to be done is the construction of two locks, one opposite where lock 18 used to be in the old Cornwall canal and the other a short distance upstream. There will then remain only the excavation between the two locks the whole of which should cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50 million.
The point I wish to make at this time is that I take issue with this statement which appears to ignore the fact that a large portion of the all-Canadian seaway is already in existence. I also wanted to take issue with it because of the fact it has been stated that Ontario hydro had built the closure in the dike at the cost of $14 million. It is true that Ontario hydro built the structure in the dike at that cost but it was done by virtue of an agreement with the federal government. By virtue of that agreement with the federal government Ontario hydro had to provide for 14-foot navigation on the Canadian side of the boundary line. When it was decided that the seaway would be built on the American side of the line in the international section, it therefore became unnecessary to provide for 14-foot navigation facilities and the agreement was amended in order that the structure be placed in the dike so that at any future time if it became necessary because of the volume of traffic the provisions would be there to complete the all-Canadian seaway.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I must advise him that his time has expired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I
believe I can complete what I have to say quickly. I had some points which I shall have to leave because of the point of order which was raised but I shall complete the thought I was expressing. While a large portion of the all-Canadian seaway has been completed, what the house, the premier of Ontario and the government should be reminded of-and I remind them of it as respectfully as I can-is that what has been done thus far has been done in co-operation with the United States and I am sure the government would want that co-operation to continue. Certainly it would want it to continue in view of the agreement which was made originally, namely that if the circumstances were such, because traffic reached such a point, that parallel or duplicating facilities were required, these could be built on the Canadian side of the line after consultation with the United States. The former government made all the provisions necessary for this to be done. I did not want the premier of the province of Ontario to make the statement he did without, at least, there being a reply to what had been said.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I came to this house last session I had hoped, like many new members, to make my opening speech on a subject that is very dear to my heart and one in which I have taken a keen interest for many years. Until this moment I have never been given the opportunity of delivering my maiden speech, as it were, on this subject but now I must thank the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) who, by means of his motion today, has made it possible for me to say something that I have dreamed of saying in the House of Commons for many years.
Before turning to an outline of the government's position with respect to a national development policy, there are a few comments which have been made by the Leader of the Opposition which should not pass unchallenged. The hon. gentleman referred to the Gordon commission and mentioned that two briefs were presented to that body, one by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories and the other by the commissioner of the Yukon. One of the later speakers read a paragraph from those submissions. By introducing that remark into this debate the barrenness of the position of the official opposition on the matter of national development has been exposed.
If you read the brief to the Gordon commission as submitted by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories, and if you read the Gordon commission report, you will find a great absence of information in the report
National Development Policy about the impact of that brief on the members of that commission. If you look at the index of the Gordon commission report you will find that the members of that commission thought that the north and the maritime provinces were so unimportant that they put them in the last chapter and grouped the two together like taking kittens and putting them in a sack along with a rock and throwing them into the river. Read that chapter in the Gordon commission report on the north and the maritimes. I would be hesitant ever to mention the Gordon commission report and the north in the same breath.
This submission to the Gordon commission by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories did mention certain things. It did mention that we should proceed with the Pine Point railway. But what the Leader of the Opposition forgot to tell this house was that no decision was made by the previous government to go ahead with the Pine Point railway. My department got no encouragement to make such a proposal which was necessary to the opening up of such a vast area of our country. The facts tell the story. The Pine Point railway was never recommended by the government of this country and I do not think we would have got a recommendation as long as the previous administration stayed in office. I will come to that in a minute.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke also of the fact that these two submissions to the royal commission outlined a grid system of roads in the territories. That is precisely true, but once again the record is clear and plain. The men in the department, some of them with a generation of interest in work in the north, put their hearts, their knowledge and their courage into suggestions that would build this country but year after year they saw their suggestions filed away in the brief cases and in the filing cabinets of their department. They saw their work, sometimes done at great difficulty and danger to themselves, pushed aside in the interest of looking after the people who lived in what the previous government called Canada where there is somebody. What they meant by "there is somebody" are nothing else but plain voters, with no thought of the future of the children of those voters. It was an appeal to their prejudice and their selfishness in the hope of being re-elected over and over again.
That is an awful statement to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I have the record here. In this submission to the royal commission there is a recommendation for roads.

National Development Policy
It is a dreadful thing for the minister to make a statement like that.
You don't like it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I look at the record of expenditures. I look to the pledge that the former government made for the development of this road pattern in the north. I find that in 1954-55 the previous government, always interested in the north, spent the magnificent sum of $2,501 in the territories; in the year 1955-56 it spent the sum of $86,770 on roads in the north. Then, in 1956-57 the amount increased, and in 1957-58, thanks to the extra boost that we gave it last winter, the amount reached $3.8 million, and for 1958-59 it is still $3.8 million, but a big proportion of that vote is on planning and surveys to complete a grid system through the Northwest Territories, recommended by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories, to extend until 1980 as a program for the government, but this government plans to do it in from five to seven years. That is the difference on emphasis on these northern roads.
I did not bother to bring the figures for the Yukon. Suffice it to say this, Mr. Speaker. In this year in the Yukon the expenditure on roads and bridges and similar construction, such as culverts and so on, is four times greater than it was last year and that pace will be kept up until in five years we have a road right through to the Arctic ocean, the first in Canada's history, laying claim to our country along that coast, which should have been done many years ago.
I might digress for a moment to point out that after all the years that those pioneer people have been in the north with very little radio and very little news of the rest of this country, a decision was made just recently to send Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's programs into the north with the building of a big transmitter at Vancouver and eventually one at Winnipeg and a series of 12 small transmitters, scattered through the north.
Who were the pioneers of the C.B.C. in this country, not the hon. gentleman opposite?
The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, and you know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Before this debate is over there will be many diversions thrown across our trail. If anyone thinks he can get me off this subject by mentioning the C.B.C. he is sadly mistaken.

The minister mentioned the C.B.C.
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The pioneers to whom I am referring are the people living in the north who wanted to hear some news of this country. We have made a recommendation to the C.B.C. and have gone forward and brought this news and entertainment to them.
I want to go on and mention just a few more points and I shall move rapidly because there are certain things 1 want to get at that are positive and in the interests of this house. The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the Liberal record and he gave as an example of that record their work and interest in water resources. Let me inform the house, that the previous administration passed the Canada Water Conservation Act in 1953 to help local districts, to help provinces develop and conserve their water in the various drainage basins of Canada. How many projects have gone forward under that act? Not one. That is an example of the Liberal record. The Canada Water Conservation Act went on the statute books in 1953 and has never been used to this day.
I go on and discuss another point.
Who controls the resources?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
As I listened to the hon. member he spoke with words of praise and mentioned the fact that the Liberals had always been in favour of northern development. He mentioned the need of establishing our sovereignty in the north. As I heard him speak what a conversion I heard. This is the same hon. gentleman who not so many months ago went up and down this country and referred to this program in the north as a program of building roads from igloo to igloo, building roads where there is nobody, and all the little echoes and all the little parts of Canada where all the little minds come from answered in tune. Here is one of those little echoes. This is a man who comes from the north, and he said: "Up there we knew it was pure baloney." That was a remark of the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie), who is a follower and supporter of the official opposition. Here is another remark from the north: "The good northern people may have mistaken this vision for just another example of the northern lights." This is a remark by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin).
Let us have a word or two about this question of our north in so far as sovereignty is concerned. This is a subject which must appeal to all Canadians, regardless of political conviction; this is a subject which must appeal to all those who believe in the future of this nation. Sovereignty is not painting a colour on a map that you publish and put in a history

book or geography book and let the children in the schools look at it and read it.
Sovereignty is the effective occupation of an area by a country which has command or control over it. It is no misstatement of fact that it is a matter of national chagrin to some of us that across this, our territory, which we paint in red in the geography books and show to our children as Canada, roads have been built without our permission and without our knowledge by people not bearing allegiance to this country. It is a matter of common knowledge that this whole northern area is an area of much interest to the world and it is a matter of chagrin to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that when I want information on the northern part of my country I have to read documents from other countries. Our friends to the south and our friends to the north have more knowledge about the northern region of our country than we who live in the country have.
May I ask the minister a question? Is he suggesting that the Russians have more knowledge of our Arctic than we have?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: If the Leader of the Opposition will follow carefully the words of the Arctic institute, a group supported by both the United States and ourselves, he will find this country condemned for knowing so little about the north when Russia knows so much.

Their own north, not our
north, surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: It is no secret that when we want to find out the depth of the water off our coast we go to Russian charts.

I suppose that is why you
decommissioned the Labrador.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I say that is a matter of national chagrin. I want to point out that at our present rate of progress in measuring the depth of the waters off our northern shores it will take us 250 years to know how deep those waters are. It is a matter of national chagrin that with the great need for this information we have not the facilities to get it fast enough. I simply point out that when any person starts to talk in the house about the question of sovereignty in the north this is a matter that appeals to all Canadians and there is no political division on this point. If we are to maintain our sovereignty in the north we must face up to the fact that we all have a duty and a responsibility to pay the price in order to get this information so that we will know something about our own country.
National Development Policy
The main point made by the Leader of the Opposition was that there was no hurry to develop the wealth of the north. He mentioned casually the Paley report and the Gordon commission and said that they indicated that there was going to be a deficiency in the United States in respect of certain strategic materials and energy fuels. Then he went on to say, "We will wait until the demand comes and then we will move."
If he would read the submission of the commissioner of the Northwest Territories to the Gordon commission he would find there the answer to that argument. In the north you must move five to ten years in advance before these great sources of wealth can be made available. He will also find that we have to have some consideration for the people who live in the north. If there is anything that has divided this country it is the frustration that pioneer people have felt at all times in our history towards those in government controlling their destinies because of their lack of consideration for the men who first went into these areas.
From the history of this country I could relate example after example. I could tell of how the people of western Ontario rose in revolt in 1833 and 1838 on that same issue of frustration and neglect of their needs. I could speak of the dissatisfaction of the people of western Canada in 1870 and 1885 at the neglect we suffered at the hands of those who had control over much of our destiny. In the same way it is true in the north that those who have pioneered there have a sense of frustration and neglect in that even after representations are made on their behalf by men who at least know something of their problems they are still overlooked.
It strikes me that the Leader of the Opposition is in this position. He is the leader of a party which is in the wilderness and as their Moses he must seek for a message to bring to the people. But I should like to suggest that in this case he is a Moses without a message. Never in the history of the nation has it been so imperative that we do not overlook the opportunities before us, not only the development of our national wealth but the mere basic fact of maintaining our sovereignty so that generations to follow will have the future to which they are entitled. These matters demand tremendous interest in the north and this interest is not divorced from the needs of the people in the settled areas of Canada and the largest cities. I hope to make that clear.
Before leaving the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, may I deal with what he had to say about an investment program. To listen to various members of the opposition one would think that the government has

National Development Policy given no thought to the matter of public and private investment and the interplay of forces between them. I hope that my remarks, and I will give some figures, will indicate to the Leader of the Opposition that a great deal of thought has been given to the question of public investment, its expansion and contraction and what it has to do with the over-all economics of the country in the present economic situation. I hope that as a result of my remarks some of these statements about the north will not be made in the future because they do harm to the interests of Canada.
The development of the north is not divorced from the needs of the people of every one of our towns and communities throughout settled Canada. I should like to discuss in detail some of the other observations he made but I think I will leave it at that.
I want to start now on the speech I have waited to make for a long time.
I hope it will be more accurate than what has happened so far.
I hope the hon. gentleman is not going to start with George Brown.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I will have a word about George Brown in a minute.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It will not be with Pickersgill anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Over the years some of us in the Conservative party have advocated a development policy for Canada. We played our part in the convention of 1948 and again in the convention of 1956. To many of us the election of 1957 was the vindication of a policy for which we had worked for a quarter of a century. We knew instinctively that the one thing that could distinguish this party and enable it to fulfil its destiny in the political history of Canada was for it to turn its attention to its great historic mission in Canada, the development of Canada and the building of a nation in the northern half of this continent truly patterned on our own way of life. The last parliament, which was short, was a period of getting ready. I would have liked, if there had been a second session of that parliament-
So would we.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
-to introduce many of the proposals which have since been introduced. I should like to refer to a few of them as found in the opening campaign speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) made in Winnipeg on February 12. I want to list ten points taken from the report of the speech as found in a Canadian Press dispatch in the Edmonton Journal of February 13, 1958. Here are the ten points of the
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle).1
development program as outlined at that time. It is the first time they have been placed on the records of the House of Commons and I am very proud to do so. They are:
1.	A $100 million roads program in the Yukon and Northwest Territories to open exploration of new oil and mineral areas.
2.	A joint federal-provincial plan to build access roads to the north, tying in with the Territories roads, costing $75 million and perhaps double that amount if all provinces join the program.
3.	Federal aid to "economically-sound" rail lines to resources, including the proposed Pine Point railway from northern Alberta to Great Slave lake.
4.	Exploration of the Arctic archipelago aimed at developing Arctic sea routes "with the prospect of developing atomic icebreakers in the future."
5.	A 10-year, $105 million scheme for thermal power plants in the Atlantic provinces, provided in legislation last session.
6.	A $75 million development at Frobisher Bay on Baffin island, in the Arctic.
Then, seventh, there is the possible second route for the trans-Canada highway in western Canada via Saskatoon and Edmonton; eighth, the federal sharing in Saskatchewan's power-irrigation development of the South Saskatchewan river; ninth, Canada would also press for hydro power development of British Columbia's Columbia river, now awaiting an agreement with the U.S. on the sharing of downstream power benefits; and, tenth, a national conference would be called later this year to map a national conservation policy. The principles of the prairie farm rehabilitation plan, begun in the 1930's in the west, would be extended to all parts of Canada. I have read the points-
Are those items covered in the estimates for the present fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I was going to deal with them in detail, and I would be answering the hon. member's question.
I do not think there are any of them in the estimates. Those are all part of the vision.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I have read to the house the ten points mentioned at that time. Now I should like to give some of the reasons why those ten points are mentioned, and this is the point I want to drive home to every Canadian who hears or reads these remarks.
We have in Canada as a national task the necessity of delineating our resources. If any person knows the history of modern industrial states he will find that their whole success or failure rests upon the supply and regulation of energy sources. We have neither an inventory nor a continuing inventory or any form of usable data of our energy resources in Canada. We do have some knowledge of our resources, but it is

incomplete. We do have knowledge of potential gas reserves, but that is far from complete. We do have some knowledge of propane and butane, but very little information is available on these subjects. We do have some knowledge of our coal reserves; we do have some knowledge of our uranium and nuclear energy, but we have much to learn about other energy sources. It must have been clear to any person who was thinking-
I am rising on a point of order. I am sure the leader on the other side will agree with me it is very difficult to relate the minister's remarks now to the motion before the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will hear the minister who presumably has some justification for his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I think the hon. member is being facetious, Mr. Speaker.
Not at all, sir, I was most serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Assuming the point of order was serious, Mr. Speaker, I say that anyone will realize that because the government has been elected on its basic development program it is in order for me to put on the record our reasons for embarking on such a national development program in order to make clear every one of those points I have raised.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The only hesitation I have about the minister's speech is that the amendment appears to be limited to the settled areas of Canada. The reference is that in northern Canada as well government measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital, especially in the form of transportation facilities, municipal improvements, and the field of small business has been added by the other amendment, and other facilities to stimulate the economic development and to promote social well-being in the settled areas of Canada. It seems fairly broad, and 1 doubt if it would be possible to limit discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think if you had been present at the beginning you would have realized that the Leader of the Opposition in introducing his amendment spent most of his time on the question that we were foolish to do anything in the north at the present time.

I never made any such
statement. I would not like that to go on the record. I said, and the minister must remember, that we would be foolish to go
National Development Policy ahead with projects in the north unless we gave them careful economic consideration, and I quoted the minister in approval of that approach.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
We will leave it at that. I was discussing the reasons why we introduced this program. The first thing, and I will repeat this, was to delineate our resources in both the fields of energy and strategic materials. I should like to mention the Paley report. The significance to Canada of the Paley report, outlined in five volumes, is the fact that strategic materials and energy fields in the United States are getting into a precarious position. Various metals and various sources of energy will either run out or become limited at different times. Generally speaking, this is the position. The United States today, instead of being a resource surplus country is a resource deficit country, and the present percentage is given at nine per cent. In a few years from now, 1975 or 1980, it is expected the United States will be running 20 per cent behind their ordinary needs for resources.
Now this means that the people of the United States, both public and private investors, must seek different places in the world from which they can replenish those needs and maintain their industrial machine. Obviously the place to look is to the north and to the south, and they are doing just that. I point out that today Canada is one of the last great resource areas, still unexplored and undeveloped. The Leader of the Opposition would have us move cautiously before we find out anything about these resources in case we repeat the mistake made 60 years ago in the building of two railways across Canada at the time of the Laurier government.
The first purpose, Mr. Speaker, was to delineate these resources, and the reason for that is obvious. When we have the resources that the world needs, we should know where they are and of what they consist. This is the first purpose of the program of roads to resources. We have to know what we have. We have no inventory and we have no group of people fully qualified or able to look after them. When this government took office and met this house on October 14, 1957 the first thing it did was to set up a royal commission on energy called the Borden commission. This royal commission, and this national energy board are 10 years overdue. I have heard suggestions that we do not need a national energy board; that the federal power commission in Washington knows enough about these resources that we can take their advice. If this is the attitude of Canadians, if this is the attitude of the majority of members on this side of the
1982	HOUSE OF
National Development Policy house, they should not be here. I am sure they do not believe it. We want and we need a national energy board. The Gordon commission has recommended it, and it is 10 years overdue.
Any government that sat here from 1945 onwards without recognizing the need tor some form of national energy board was unaware of or completely indifferent to the suggestions that are made all across this country. This country today stands completely helpless in this respect. We have no body of opinion here in Canada qualified to say whether we should export or import energy, whether we should delineate more of our resources or whether we should hold it back. There is no such board or body available here in this country.
I now want to go on, Mr. Speaker, to some of the details of these roads to resources, in answering the point made by the Leader of the Opposition, and I hope that he takes these figures to heart. I am going to give him an example of public investment and private investment interrelated. This projected road from Flat creek in the Yukon, 30 miles this side of Dawson city, projecting north and northeastward to the Arctic coast some place in the neighbourhood of Fort McPherson,will be finished in the next four or five years. It will cost the people of this country between $5 million and $8 million in a five-year period. Is this house aware of the fact that already behind that road private investment has pledged in hard dollars and cents a minimum expenditure, I would estimate, of something about $150 million to $250 million? As the hon. member was speaking I sent over for the latest information. Let him read these facts. Let him tell the people of Canada that this is a road from igloo to igloo. Since September 23 when I notified the oil and gas industry of our change in regulations pending with respect to exploration for oil and gas in the territories, permits for the exploration of 36,452,214 acres of land have been taken out in the Northwest Territories, mostly along the route of this road.

Did the hon. gentleman
not say that the road was in the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Starting in the Yukon and going into the Northwest Territories. I might add some more figures. Before September 23 last land for which permits were taken out and reservations made amounted roughly to 20 million acres. If you add all these things together you get a figure much higher than the one I have just quoted. I have put these figures in the public record, Mr. Speaker because I think the mere restatement of them is sufficient to show the situation. If the taxpayer is asked to put up
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1

$5 million or $8 million in public investment in this area, and if private investment from all over the world is willing to risk a sum extending up to $250 million, I would say as a minimum, it shows that that investment was timely, was well thought out and was made with due caution. I used the word "minimum". Of course information comes to me that is not available to the house.
I used that word advisedly. I am going to ask my fellow colleagues on this side of the house to remember this one little fact. During the election campaign to my knowledge, no member on the government side including the Prime Minister ever used a figure higher than $25 million to $50 million as the expected investment of private enterprise. That was my advice to the Prime Minister last February, namely that the expected amount of private investment for exploration in this area was $25 million to $50 million. But I now stand here in the middle of the summer of 1958 and inform this house that the bare minimum will be between $150 million and $250 million.
That was announced in this house about three years ago.
Oh, oh.
It was announced by Mr. Howe three years ago as a possible estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not finished yet. We have another project going into the north which is to tie up with the territorial program in the north, that of going to the provinces and asking them to join with us in providing roads leading into the north. At the time the Prime Minister spoke in Winnipeg he estimated that $75 million would be spent on this program over a five-year period. We had no way of knowing how willing the provinces would be in cooperating with the federal government in the opening of resource areas in their provinces where they, the provinces, owned the resources and had complete responsibility for their management. Since the Prime Minister spoke, it is now no secret that nine provinces have joined up in the scheme and not only have they asked for amounts which will send the total up to the maximum but they have asked for amounts that go beyond the maximum. I think the people of Canada in all the provinces will be proud to know that their provincial governments are co-operating with the federal government in this program of making resources available to the people of Canada for opportunity and development at this time.
Another one of these programs was the Pine Point railway. I hope the Leader of the

Opposition will listen to these figures. There has been no secret about the fact that that railway will cost between $60 million and $65 million. Obviously, as is traditional, the federal government will be asked to put up a subsidy. It is quite possible that subsidy can be measured-using millions of dollars-on the fingers of two hands. That will be our contribution as a people and as taxpayers. But there are facts that are not generally known, Mr. Speaker. The total of public and private investment on this Pine Point railway is not $65 million in the ties, the bridges and the steel rails; the total investment at the present time is reaching the figure of $400 million. This government has letters of intent from private business with respect to putting up private capital to the amounts roughly that I have just indicated. If at any time any government can spend a handful of millions of dollars and produce so many tens of millions of dollars of private investment, then I say that government is aware of the relationship between public investment and private investment.
I see that the clock shows that it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had been discussing the reasons why we had to inaugurate in Canada a program of delineating our resources both with regard to energy and with regard to strategic metals. I mentioned how as the first step in this program we had inaugurated a program of building a big system of roads in the territories to help delineate both the oil and the metallic ores. I spoke next of the uselessness of building a great system of roads in the territories unless there were roads in the south to join them to the settled areas. I spoke, too, of the necessity for moving carefully with regard to these programs, and I gave some examples where the public taxpayer was asked to spend several millions of dollars which resulted in many millions of dollars being advanced by private enterprise to carry out their part of this joint public and private investment program.
The main point which, I think, the Leader of the Opposition made in the course of his remarks was that the question of timing was important. I believe it is fair to say that he was aware that every Canadian knew that in the northern areas we have
National Development Policy tremendous wealth, but that we should wait until the economics of the need for these materials are absolutely clear before any program is started to open them up. I countered by referring to the statement made by the commissioner for the Northwest Territories to the Gordon commission in 1955 in which he developed the argument that in the north when you needed resources you have to begin five or ten years before they could be made available to the economy of the country. I should like to emphasize this point by reminding the house that the preliminary report indicates that by 1975 or 1980 in the great republic to the south the shortage of certain raw materials will be quite urgent. The report specifically mentions certain strategic metals and it is believed that the great industrial machine in the United States will be facing severe difficulties in obtaining supplies.
We in the northern half of this continent have a responsibility to our people. We are sitting here on what is probably the greatest treasure house of the world; certainly, there is only one nation that can rival us in this respect, and that is the U.S.S.R. If we sit here and wait for prices to rise above their normal economic level to indicate to our mining people and to our oil people that it is time to move in and develop these areas, we should in my opinion be failing in our responsibility to this growing nation. I believe that if we are to have any control over the discovery and development of these resources it is in our interest that we find out and find out soon where they are, what they are and how much we have of each.
Could I ask the hon. gentleman a question? How would he find out where these resources are?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
There are several well known methods of finding out. If you are looking for oil and gas, you drill holes. If you are looking for minerals you do a certain amount of preliminary aerial reconnaissance using magnetometers and gravity meters, then you make a ground survey, and finally you have to drill holes, too.
In this delineation of resources there are three steps. The first is to discover where a deposit lies. That gives you the location, but it does not give you the extent; it gives you the type of metal you have, but it does not give you the potential or the probable reserve. Therefore, the first step in our program of opening up our resources is to build railroads, or to use water navigation or aerial navigation to find out information about an area which, by formula projection or by other devices used by survey engineers, can lead
1984	HOUSE OF
National Development Policy to an estimation of future tonnages or deposits in reserve. As a matter of fact, the province of Alberta has done a great deal of work in estimating not only its proven reserves in oil and gas but in trying to work out its potential and probable reserves. That is the only area in Canada where anything resembling an inventory has been carried out, and if we do not have an inventory we can have no policy with regard to handling these resources. That is the situation behind the national energy board set-up.
I wish to go on now to discuss further this question of research with reference to the Winnipeg speech. I do not think there is any hon. member in this house who could argue more strongly than myself in favour of the necessity for research. Here in Canada we need research not only into basic aspects of an exploration program but research into techniques concerning the handling of these minerals and energy sources.
On this question of research, I am amazed at the slow rate of progress we are making. If we keep up the present progress in Canada it will take 250 years of hydrographic survey before we find out the depths of water around the northern shores of this country. We have no gravity meter surveys of the northern islands; we have made no survey of 80 per cent of British Columbia; we have done almost nothing in the Yukon, yet this is the vital geophysical information we need in order to get some idea of the extent of our exploration program.
In the months of February, March and April, representatives of this country attended a meeting of the United Nations in Geneva on the international code of law for the sea, and at that meeting one of a series of resolutions passed, which was accepted by the majority of the nations present, dealt with the continental shelf.
The first of those three resolutions or conventions denied the right of any nation to attach reservations to them. I am very proud to report that this country, through its representatives there, played a very active part both in proposing the resolution and in establishing the fact that no nation could attach to that reservation. This grants to this country with land off its shores not only the right to develop and explore the territory but the right to exploit it to the degree one can with the improving techniques of this day and age. The advantage to our country of this natural resource area is hard to estimate. I have used the figure of 25 per cent although it may be 20 per cent or more than 25 per cent. But if the country acquired a territory of an additional 25 per cent by the ordinary means of acquiring land it would cause great headlines in our press. Quietly,


at this meeting of the United Nations, meeting for peaceful purposes, we added to our resources an area of tremendous acreage. I point this out because it emphasizes the need for research in this country by means of which we can measure the mineral and oil potential of these lands beneath the sea.
It may interest hon. members to know that the techniques of exploration beneath the sea are improving almost month by month. We think we have an answer to the question of conducting gravity meter surveys by vessels on the surface of the ocean. We also think we have an answer to the question of conducting gravity meter surveys by using helicopters. This will assist in overcoming the difficulties we presently encounter in working in a troublesome terrain. As I have said, I mention these things to emphasize the need for research in the north. As a younger Canadian I quite frankly admit I am somewhat ashamed that with all the effort and energy many of us expended on this question last year we were able to mount during the summer of 1958 a research program in the Arctic costing only approximately $50,000. That can be found in the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I should like to have seen a sum ten times that large but I hope and expect that if we can get the men and equipment mounted we will have ready for next year a program costing in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars for research in that area alone. Even with that amount being expended it will take us years to acquire the vital information we require on which we can base an extensive exploration program of the far northern islands.
Some of you here may wonder why it is that these far northern islands are of such interest to us. There are many reasons and I could possibly best illustrate my point by mentioning Frobisher Bay. Frobisher Bay is situated on the southern part of Baffin island. Baffin island is an island which in years to come will become as well known to Canadians as is the Mesabi range to the people of the United States. It was on the basis of the development of the Mesabi range in the United States that the great industrial economy of that nation was built. From the information that we have available-I admit it is sketchy-we expect that in the whole area of the eastern Arctic we will find anywhere from two to six times the amount of iron ore that was available to the people of the United States in the Mesabi range in the last 100 years. When you are dealing with resources like that you realize that there is no time for timidity or extra caution. Not only must there be boldness but imagination as well both in the broad sense and in

the technical sense of reaching in and finding out by research and hard work how to best use these resources.
Frobisher Bay came to our attention not through anything this government did but due to the fact that it was halfway between the western coast of the United States and Canada and the capital cities of Europe. It is the natural stopping place on a direct route from the orient to the west coast of Canada and the United States and the centres of population in Europe. Therefore it has developed spontaneously and economically as a base of refuelling for commercial aircraft. At the present time in the neighbourhood of 1,500 passengers a week stop over at Frobisher Bay. It lends itself to strategic defence in the northern areas of the eastern part of the continent. Therefore, from these two sources, civilian and military, comes a source of revenue to help us finance and build up this area which in future will become the centre of administration of the eastern Arctic. But let me point out this to hon. members. Baffin island is not forever going to be financed by defence and through servicing passengers on polar routes. The basic economy is going to be iron ore and other minerals that exist on the island. This great source of wealth is accessible to ourselves and the nations of the world through sea transport. I fully expect that before many years have passed Frobisher Bay and other communities in that area will be the centre of an extremely thriving extractive industry producing iron and other minerals for Canada.
The next point in our program deals with power. On this matter I can understand the confusion of hon. members opposite. When this government took office there were three requests for assistance or aid in the development of power in Canada. One of these was in the maritime provinces. The other was on the Saskatchewan river. The third was on the rivers that make up the Columbia system. Naturally, because these were the requests before the federal government, it was on these three power development projects that the government first took action. The requests had been placed before the previous Liberal administration and all hon. gentlemen know the record in that regard. The record of the previous government was fully debated in this house in the last session of parliament with respect to the project in the maritimes and I hope the record of the request concerning the Saskatchewan river project will be discussed in this house at a later date.
I wish to say a word or two concerning the Columbia river project. It was our hope on the basis of the information we had to move quickly in working out the economics as well as the engineering aspects of the
National Development Policy Columbia river system to make this vast source of power available to the areas of western Canada and the United States where power is scarce. We thought that with a little energy and some intelligence we could advance this program very rapidly. It was not long before we discovered that we lacked the necessary information to deal effectively with the question of the Columbia river project.
I recently watched a television program emanating from the United States during which the United States head of the international joint commission pointed out that the United States people had the figures on the Columbia river project for the last 25 years and that Canada did not have the figures. That, Mr. Speaker, is the answer. When you begin to deal with the resources of a great international river like the Columbia you do not enter a game of that sort playing with the cards of the fellow across the table. We had to get figures based on Canadian engineering and economics. We have put the energy and intelligence to work on this project. I can assure the house that at this time we are coming very close to knowing what figures we have and what the economics as well as the engineering facts are, and that we are moving toward a position where we can enter into any negotiation that may take place with all the facts at our command that we require to ensure that this great wealth and resource which is Canada's will be protected to the fullest extent in the national interest.
How did you learn the facts?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: My hon. friend asks me how I learned the facts. They were gleaned from engineering reports which were started about two years ago.
By the former ministry.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
That is true. They were learned by the economic studies which we have undertaken and I recall last session when the then member for Montma-gny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) asked me in this house why I did not go down to the United States and have more powwows with them, I just thought of an old rhyme that we used to sing to ourselves during the days of the first world war:
Kaiser Bill went up the hill To take a look at France;
Kaiser Bill came down the hill With bullets in his pants.
That is what happened to the previous minister of northern affairs and national resources when he went to discuss without the facts and figures, and that would have happened to the present minister if he had gone there unprepared and without the arms-

National Development Policy
What new surveys or economic surveys has the minister started since June 23 of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
The hon. member will find out the answer very shortly. One was started in the month of January, 1958, and that is the one I was referring to. I just mentioned this fact about the Columbia to show that here is another great resource where the Americans can speak on their national television hookups and boast that they have had the information for 25 years, and the Canadians have not. I am simply pointing out that we have not the facts in Canada as yet; we are still getting them.
The next point I would like to discuss in this over-all program is this. Our first purpose was to delineate those resources and discuss research and the necessity for it. I have used the example of Frobisher Bay. We are moving into the north and carefully, with great planning, to take advantage of the situation as it now is, but thinking forward to the day when the economics of the area, of mining, will support that whole community and other communities as well. I could have taken a good deal of time of the house to point out the efforts we have made in research to cut down the cost of heating homes, to cut down the cost of providing water for those homes, to cut down the cost of providing sewer services for those homes. I could tell the house, as I told the committee in another place, of the amount of savings that we think we have achieved already by simply applying the basic knowledges of engineering and economics to very simple mundane problems.
I know that this is not the end of our difficulties but it does show that we are going into this with great care and great planning. One of the final points is the question of conservation mentioned by the Prime Minister. I know hon. members will understand me when I say that it is only by the grace of the divine Deity Himself that we have been saved in this regard.
If one looks at the history of the economic development of the United States and realized the great importance of the contribution of the first Roosevelt to the handling of the resources of that great American republic, one will recognize the significance of the step that we are now prepared to take. Conservation of resources means the best and most efficient use of those resources. It means that all the facts of wild life, of power, of land, of water, of various minerals, of the forest industry, the health of our people, all these assets which make up our resources in this country are put together

and looked at and certain principles evolved, principles under which the federal government must operate; principles under which the provincial governments must operate; principles under which municipal governments must operate; principles under which regional conservation boards must operate; principles under which the research people of our universities must operate, and all those many public-spirited citizens who make up the great rank and file of our conservation groups in Canada. This country has never sat down and established over a wide range of resources a fundamental policy on the handling of those natural resources. After I spoke on this program last fall for the first time my mail came in from many sources, from the universities, from the people interested in wild life and in forests, from people interested in minerals and from people interested in the forest industry, and from people interested in land uses. They pointed out to me how pleased they were that at last somebody was giving direction to this program.
We have written the provinces on this matter; we have been in touch with other departments and I would like to say that this conservation conference will possibly be going forward this fall; but such has been the multitude of suggestions, and such has been the volume of old reports that we have stacked up, trying to study what has been done in the past, and such has been the tremendous complexity of this whole problem, that I have confessed publicly I doubt the wisdom of calling the conservation conference next fall. More likely it will be some time next spring or next summer when we can have the agenda boiled down and crystallized to the point where the people who can assemble there can take a worthwhile forward step. On this question of conservation, if this government comes forward with this program of calling the people of Canada together who are interested in the most efficient use of the resources, and does come out in the next three or four years with a series of principles that can guide all levels of government and private groups in the future, if it does nothing more, it would be well worth the confidence of the people of Canada for many years to come.
I have spoken at some length on this program, Mr. Speaker, because above all this is the one feature of this government that distinguishes it from the official opposition.
The only one.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
If we are to
embark on a program of national development not only must we draw the first faint lines on a blueprint and carefully fill out

the lines that go step by step in natural sequence, but we must know where we are heading and where we are heading is in this direction. We think that some day we will have on the northern half of this continent a nation of from 50 million to 100 million people. If we are to have a nation of 100 million people in Canada, then it is about time we did some thinking about how this is going to come about. There is no use talking about all the oil resources under the continental plains reaching out into the Arctic and out under the Arctic ocean, and possibly under the lands beneath the sea in the Arctic; it is no use talking about our wonderful wealth of forests-and it is wonderful-it is no use talking about all the future mineral wealth; it is no use talking about the great character of our people unless we put these things side by side, with our people as one part of the equation and their energy sources another part of the equation, and those various other resources such as minerals and forests. We must put this energy to work.
If we act so that the energy, the natural resources and our people in this equation are opened up to private enterprise so that by the juxtaposition of those resources and this power and of those people and of this market there is an economic development possible in that area, I think we would be measuring up to the philosophy that this government holds concerning private enterprise and public expenditure. Or, to put it another way, we believe that the state, the government, has the duty and responsibility to provide that social capital mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition in his amendment, in the form of roads, railways, power plants, airports and all those things that aid and benefit private enterprise to enter in and develop those resources for the good of the people of Canada. If we point out in this House of Commons where we spend money in public investment to yield much larger investments by private enterprise, I think we have demonstrated down to earth principles of good, sound government, following a philosophy which we see quite clearly. If we are to be measured in the future by the tests of history it will be by what extent we succeed or fail in building processing industries here in Canada.
There is iron in Labrador, iron in Baffin island, iron in Ungava, iron in the western Arctic. It is of no use to us if it all goes to feed the industrial plants of nations all over the world so that we in Canada can buy back the finished products. We will have to export tremendous millions of tons to all these countries because that is part of our responsibility in the world but we must make
National Development Policy sure that large supplies are available to be manufactured and processed here in Canada without increasing the cost. But on the contrary, because of the juxtaposition of energy and natural resource, produced here cheaper than in any other part of the world, in the decades ahead we will be the greatest supplier of iron and steel products in the world. I repeat that this must be done by careful planning and by creating situations whereby economics will result in the cheaper production that will give us an advantage on an economic basis without restraints or artificial subsidies of any kind.
I think I have made my point clear. We on this side of the house do have a national development policy. I was going to quote a question asked me last October by the former minister of northern affairs and national resources at which time he challenged me to produce this national development program right when I was busy trying to work out some of the details of it. I have sat here ever since waiting for an opportunity to give the house a few ideas of what the program is all about. You have got it now.
I am going to remind the Leader of the Opposition of a few facts about our history. The other night I mentioned casually the name of a man called Brown. This man lived roughly 100 years ago. I praised his contribution to Canadian political thought in connection with development and the opposition had great fun pointing out the fact that he also believed in legislative union. They could have pointed out a few more things about George Brown. He had other dogmatic convictions which I am going to leave unmentioned. I do not care what a man believes in every aspect of his thinking. However, I am going to put before the house just a few of his words because, wherever George Brown is now, I hope he will know that someone a century later appreciates these thoughts. I read from an editorial he wrote in the Globe roughly 100 years ago;
The non-occupation of the Northwest Territory is a blot upon our character for enterprise. We are content to play drone while others are working. We settle down quietly within the petty limits of an insignificant province while a great empire is offered to our ambition. ... If Canada acquires this territory it will rise in a few years from a position of a small and weak province to be the greatest colony any country has ever possessed, able to take its place among the empires of the earth. The wealth of 400,000 square miles of territory will flow through our waters and be gathered by our merchants, manufacturers, and agriculturists. Our sons will occupy the chief places of this vast territory, we will form its institutions, supply its rules, teach its schools, fill its stores, run its mills, navigate its streams. . . . We can beat the United States if we start at once. It is an empire we have in view and its whole export and import trade will be concentrated in the hands of Canadian merchants end manufacturers if we strike for it now.

National Development Policy
Those are the words of George Brown. He was a clear Grit. If hon. members opposite would go back to the fountainhead of the words of George Brown and forget all this division and diversion that has come along in the last 100 years they would put their party on a much sounder footing for the future and be much more in tune with the Canadian people than they are now.
It is significant, that in 1858, 100 years ago, a young man by the name of Alexander Tilloch Galt was invited to join the cabinet. He was invited to do so because he had a plan to bring confederation into being for the colonies on the northern half of this continent. It is significant that just 100 years ago in 1858 a young man from Toronto went to the west, up the Qu'Appelle river to the South Saskatchewan river and recommended that a dam be built. His name was Hind. Today, 100 years later, we may see a start on what he recommended. One hundred years ago men did have vision. They did have courage and some of them had the energy to go out and do something. It was Macdonald who led his government through those terrible 15 years of building the transcontinental railway known as the Canadian Pacific. If you read the speeches of the men in opposition at that time you see that they said, "Where does this road go? Who will ride on it? Indians and buffalo." I have seen a few "Indians" on those trains in recent years but very few buffalo.
Those were the words of caution by our Liberal friends 80 years ago. Everyone knows today that this railway through the bush and muskeg of northern Ontario has opened up a mineral industry that produces over a billion dollars of new wealth a year, that produces over a billion dollars of new forest wealth a year. That line ran through the west they talked about, through the prairies which they had defined as a desert. Now we have there one of the greatest bread baskets in the world.
Then, what horrible things they said about British Columbia. In the short time I have had since we adjourned at six o'clock I am sorry I was not able to dig up a few quotations of the things they said about British Columbia. They called it a most inhospitable land and said that people could not possibly exist there. Yet we have 22 members in the house today representing that province, and if Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba move a little faster they will soon have as many.
I mention these things to make clear the background of our thinking. As a party we felt that we should bring our party back to its traditional theme of developing and opening up the country. Naturally in starting this program we tended to think of the immediate

needs of the people of the maritimes and the prairies because they have fallen behind the national level of income. So we brought forward programs in those two parts of Canada because it was a part of our policy to bring about equality between groups and regions in Canada.
But I want now to emphasize the point that every time you spend a dollar to make power cheaper in the Atlantic provinces, bring industry there and make the people there prosperous, you help every other person in Canada. I say these things to the people in the Atlantic provinces and I say them here too. Every time you spend a dollar to bring some security of living to the people of central Saskatchewan it helps every part of Canada, not just the people of that part. As a Canadian I am very happy that much of the leadership for this type of thinking came from the city of Toronto. At times we do have some fun among ourselves referring to that city, but when the chips are down the people of Toronto have always measured up in the building of this nation. Just as George Brown said, all the benefit does get back there but I do not think we should quarrel about that because what helps one of us helps all of us.
Our program, therefore, is to build this nation by helping those regions which have fallen behind. We are doing this in the interests of Canada, but primarily to provide an opportunity for the people of this generation, our sons and daughters who are born here in the future, as well as the people who come to this great dominion. This is the fundamental social purpose behind what we are doing. I should like to recall, if I may, some of the words of men much greater than I. I have often heard a phrase by Edmund Burke quoted in this house, and that phrase is this:
If there is no vision the people perish-
I do believe, Mr. Speaker, this this government has a vision, a vision which the members of this government are determined to carry out. I am going to read the rest of the sentence I have just quoted.
If there is no vision the people perish, but if the vision is blurred, the people perish faster.

The things I have outlined here today are just the first lines on a blueprint of our future. We must not be deterred from a bold, imaginative policy for the development of Canada which would provide for the future of our children. I have been asked, why move now? I feel I have made it clear that we have no choice with all this wealth, all these resources, but to move now.
