Poor George Brown was murdered. I do not know why he was murdered. But in addition to the subamendment with reference to small businesses, on June 11 the Canadian Press carried a dispatch out of Ottawa stating this:
The government will shortly provide small busi-nesres with technical assistance but no direct loans, it was learned today.
The reluctance to provide federal credit may be a blow to retailers. They had urged the administration to set up some form of federal credit facility to help the corner store compete more effectively with the big chains and supermarkets for the customer's dollar.
Shortly after this date the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) was speaking on the west coast and from there there was a news release to the effect-or this is what I gathered from reading the news release; perhaps the Minister of Justice can correct me-that the main point of the government's program in relation to small business was that it was going to set up a technical advisory service especially to help small business in the field of research and other marketing problems. There is no use in belittling this step or program. I think it is very much worth while. As a matter of fact, I should like to go further. I note that according to tonight's newspaper it has been announced that an associate deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce has been appointed, namely Mr. James Roberts and it is speculated that he is to be the head of this branch. Whether or not he is the head of this branch, I know that in Mr. Roberts the government has a man of exceptional ability. He was a lieutenant colonel in the regiment in which I was a trooper; and as someone who had a parade of lieutenants colonels including the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) I can honestly say that Mr. Roberts as a lieutenant colonel was an exceptionally able one. If he


is going to be the man to head up this bureau I am sure he will be able to do something with it. But I would suggest that to restrict the bureau merely to technical advice and to research assistance is to limit it to too narrow a field.
I notice that the Canadian tourist association submitted a brief to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) a short time ago with regard to a tourist establishment improvement loan act, and that the very first paragraph of it states this:
The Canadian tourist association respectfully requests that the government of Canada submit to parliament legislation which will relieve Canada's tourist industry of a serious disability caused by lack of financial credit and so by such legislation make it possible for our tourist industry through expansion and modernization to compete effectively in the world tourist market.
Of course the tourist industry is only one facet of small business but obviously they feel that there is a need. One of the lessons the United States has learned and is learning about small business is that the very idea of support or aid by government for small business has a tremendous emotional appeal. I am not that partial to small business

The experience in the United States indicated that almost every year in congress, in the house of representatives or in the senate, some congressman or some senator will rush in with a bill to aid small business and usually the administration- that is the executive-manages to shift it to one side and keep it from going through both chambers until the legislative year is over. I think the reason for the appeal of small business goes back to the political position that it appeals to all. I think it might be Jeffersonian democracy in essence. It is the whole idea that the small man, working within his own scope and framework, trying to raise himself by his boot straps and to develop a small business, is perhaps the most worthy of all individuals in the whole economic framework.

In this particular matter I do not think we should allow emotion or sentiment to get in our way. The small business man has tremendous political power in both the United States and Canada. We often hear that huge corporations have great political power but the fact of the matter is that, as far as most members of parliament are concerned, they are much more easily approached by small businessmen and in their communities they hear much more about the problems of small business and the needs for help for small business.
I think one of the reasons that in Canada we have not had the pressure to help small business that has been experienced in the United States is that we are in a ten-year to fifteen-year lag behind the United States in the development of our general consciousness of what is happening in the economic framework. In the United States it has generally been discovered, as a result of a great deal of research into small business, that perhaps the fundamental weakness of small businesses is not credit or the failure or the inability to get money-although that matter ranks very high-but is just the question of lack of managerial ability or, if you want to use the favourite jargon of the businessman, lack of know-how. There is no doubt about it that some form of advisory bureau might be of some aid. As a matter of fact the government has published a very handy little manual of advice for the small businessman.
However, the factor of money is quite vital. In the United States the small business administration has been operating for five or six years. It now has a capitalization, I understand, of $230 million. The largest loan that a small businessman or a small manufacturer can obtain at the present time from this small business administration is $300,000, although efforts are being made to raise this amount to $500,000. One of the other points in connection with these loans is that no manufacturer or anyone else can get a loan from the small business administration unless he can produce proof that he has already been rejected by the banks at least twice or at least by two different banks, which means that the businessman has gone through some effort anyway to obtain his money from other sources. Usually the interest rate on these loans varies from 4| per cent to 6 per cent, depending on the kind of background or collateral that is available to the small businessman. In essence, when you compare the total value of the United States gross national product and their annual investment, the small business administration has not been a fantastic success. After all, $230 million is not a great deal in an economy such as that of the United States.

But there are more and more indications that help for small businesses is necessary because of the fact that large corporations have such great advantages in financing, especially in debenture financing, over small business and because on the market side of their operations they have advertising budgets that can cover a whole national field. I think that point applies particularly in Canada. In Canada our small manufacturers tend to compete regionally and it is very difficult for a small manufacturer or even a small service organization to spread beyond its region because of this lack of advertising. In the manufacturing industry it is especially difficult for them to spread and develop further because of the lack of research facilities. Advertising and research are built into the operations of large corporations.
In the particular area from which I come, namely the lakehead, we have had a tremendous change in our business structure in the last 20 years; and if you take it over the last 30 years, the change has been even greater. Thirty or forty years ago the lake-head's primary industry was tied in with transportation and being an entrepot between the west and the east. Naturally we had these large organizations, the transcontinental railways and very large shipping lines. But in our indigenous industry we depended upon the bush and woods products. In most cases those organizations were fairly small.
But now that situation has changed drastically with the buildup of the tremendous capital formations that are necessary to support pulp and paper mills, and these very large corporations have developed through using crown leases of very large limits of land. One of the results has been that the role of the small timber operator has almost disappeared except as a jobber living from hand to mouth and from year to year, very much dependent on the good will he may have developed with the particular large company concerned, and in that particular field all these small jobbers and operators are up against a tremendous financial problem when it comes to buying equipment. The breakdown of one large cat or Drott loader can make the difference between a successful operation and being completely wiped off the books. One of the reasons for this is that they have to carry so much credit at a very high rate of interest to obtain these capital goods, or else they cannot obtain loans of sufficient size and at a decent rate of interest to enable them to keep their equipment up to a proper and economic level.
In addition, at the lakehead we have noticed another phenomenon which has happened all across the country, and that

National Development Policy is the disappearance of the family store, especially the family department store, and the moving into the area of the large chains. We now have Loblaws, and A. & P. and supermarts and all the rest, and from the reaction of the population to these stores I gather that they are popular; I do not believe anyone consciously wants to go back to the small establishments we had formerly. But this displacement of the small operator has pinpointed the difficulties of people in the retail trade who are not tied in with national organizations such as Simpsons-Sears or Eatons in competing and operating in our economy. It seems to me that at the present time we have to examine the situation and try to make up our minds whether these small businesses are worth helping, and I think the answer that most of us will arrive at is that they are. There is nothing wrong with a large organization just because it is large, but there is something wrong in Canada in the fact that so many large corporations are putting small business organizations out of business.

We do not make a practice in this house of asking, say, Conservative members from Ontario to defend the policies of the provincial government with respect, for example, to the Northern Ontario Gas Company, and I hope the hon. member will extend the same courtesy to me.
I asked whether the C.C.F. policy had changed.

It has been suggested, Mr. Speaker, that the C.C.F. has climbed on to the bandwagon. We have not seen much of a bandwagon as far as small business is concerned, but I am glad to recognize that there is some merit in this policy of help for small business.

One of the other problems which is very evident at the lakehead is that whenever a small manufacturer does develop his plant and his organization to the point where he can expand his market area he discovers that just at that time he is invaded, usually by a larger organization that comes in and seeks to buy him out. That happened to a rather efficient concrete block factory that was developed by local people and had reached a very promising stage of development. Just when they were ready for a further step in expansion they were approached by a much larger factory from the Winnipeg area which pushed into this market and finally tried to force them to sell out to them at a price which was of great disadvantage to them. They were very anxious to expand in order to meet this threat, but they ran into the standard difficulty of not being able to raise enough capital to expand their plant so that they could compete. Here was an excellent case for small loans being available under the scheme suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) in this house about ten days ago. If such a scheme had been in operation they would have been in a much better position to have carried out that particular expansion.
Another fact that will probably raise certain questions from certain hon. members in certain parts of the house and one which I think needs to be faced frankly is that small manufacturers as they are developing their organizations, just when they reach a stage where they are moving from a small operation to a medium-sized operation, have discovered that they have become attractive to a union or to a union organizer, and just at a time when capital difficulties are most severe they find they are faced with the problem of signing an agreement or a contract which would require them to spend money beyond what they had planned as far as normal operating expenditures are concerned. This happened in connection with a veneer plant in the Port Arthur constituency. Just at the time when it was ready to expand it was faced with negotiating a contract with a union that wanted to nail this very small operation down to the same standards as those of much larger units in the pulp and paper industry in that area. In this particular case it was possible, through a little discretion on the part of the union, to stave off almost immediate bankruptcy for the company, but the man in charge of the company made the point that his primary difficulty was not that he did not want to meet the conditions which the union presented but that he was operating on so much borrowed capital at such a high rate of interest that it just was not feasible or economic for him to do so. He

is one of the people who made the point that he very definitely needs some form of loan for small business backed by the government.
Now the hon. member for Vancouver East made the point quite clearly: in Canada we have a situation different from that in the United States in that we have a branch banking system. The point has also been made that we already have a semi-framework to work on in something that the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) took a certain amount of credit for, that is, the Liberal institution of the industrial development bank. Since we have this situation there seems no reason why this example could not be pushed further, using the bank and setting up loans of a relatively short term- I suppose five to ten years would be the maximum on them-at relatively low rates of interest, I imagine somewhere between 6 and 8 per cent as a maximum, and that some sort of guarantee should be given by the government to the lending institutions.
The experience of the banks since moving into the mortgage lending field in connection with the national housing program has not been disastrous in any sense although a possible disaster was preached and forecast by some of the opponents of that legislation. As a matter of fact, the banks have successfully operated in this field although I know there are certain qualifications from the point of view that it does tend to tie down some of their money for longer terms than usual and in areas that are not quite as fluid as the banks perhaps might like.
All these examples tend to suggest that a good case could be made for setting up a small business administration scheme with a loan fund to be administered by the chartered banks and with the loans at least to a certain percentage guaranteed by the federal government. This might be of great advantage to the small businessmen in our community.
There are a number of other possible steps that might be taken to help small business that are not related to the establishment of a loan system. One that has been suggested is that the scale of income tax for small business be set at a less progressive rate than for larger corporations, on a graduated scale such as applies as far as personal income tax is concerned. The difficulty in that situation would be attempting to define what is a small business and probably in setting certain levels at which the tax would move upward, you would leave the door open for a certain amount of finagling on the part of the concern to keep below the level.
Another suggestion that has been made as a means of helping small business will probably be discussed very fully when the 57071-3-126

There is no question but that when there is a death in a family which operates a family organization or manufacturing concern-be it the death of one of the partners or perhaps the sole owner-the death duties in many cases lead to the dissolution of the whole business. We had a very fine family department store in Fort William that suffered the loss of its family head a few years ago. It was amazing how quickly the whole thing went to pieces and the store is now in the hands of a national concern. There is nothing the matter with that but the fact remains that the children of this gentleman were simply not able to carry on the business and also meet the death duties. With a certain amount of pleasure, Mr. Speaker. I always feel that when you engage in a discussion of a topic such as small business or small businessmen it gives a great opportunity for a discussion revolving around the whole question of free enterprise. now have. Of course, if this Jeffersonian attitude-I call it that-of myself and the other members of the C. C. F. is free enterprise and if we be damned for that, well, let us be damned, but I do not think there is anything in it that is antithetical to socialism as I certainly know it. The particular views of Jefferson have a great deal that appeal to me, but not the view that every 20 years there should be a bloody revolution. Mind you, I think Jefferson is one exemplar for almost anyone interested in politics, because he does show the value of keeping things on a small scale wherever possible, and that whole idea can be taken into account on such questions as centralization of our constitution, or the provincialist approach. Of great importance as far as business is concerned is that Jefferson himself always was aware of the point that the larger the business grows, the farther away it gets from the roots in a certain community, the more difficult it is to control and the less appeal it has for the people whom it is serving. I certainly think that at the present time we are being served by far too many large corporations who through their advertising agencies are engineering our wants. I do not think we are being served nearly enough by small groups, small business and small manufacturing organizations who can be closer to and more intimate with us.
There is one other aspect of this whole program of small business. Not only have we ignored small business in recent decades, or not only has small business fallen by the wayside, but the whole idea of public business and public service has fallen by the wayside, and we are quite justified in including in the gross national product such things as the manufacture of a tremendous number of cars and a tremendous variety of cosmetics, great wealth in terms of alcohol or, as the Toronto Star would call it, booze; but we do not really feel that developments such as roads, better schools, better hospitals, things like these, are part of genuine production. We somehow feel that they are not quite as worth while, or as profitable. That is why I think that if I 57071-3-126i

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up very much time of the house tonight. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) in a very able, in fact a brilliant speech, tonight outlined to the house and to the country what the government is doing to make the vision a reality. Today I think can be classified, because of the speeches we have heard from the opposition, as bandwagon day. The Liberals, at long last, after 22 years of neglect, are trying to climb aboard the national development bandwagon. They have found out that the people like the idea of their country being developed nationally and they are trying to clamber aboard. Then we see the C.C.F. climbing aboard the free enterprise bandwagon. Now they are grasping to their breasts small business as though they had always been brothers. They are trying to out-free-enterprise the free enterprisers. I guess one of these days we will see the formation-I understand there are feelers out on both sides now for a new party, the Liberal-Socialist party. They are trying to get together and in that way perhaps stop going down together. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources dealt very ably and brilliantly with what this government is doing in the way of national development.
I am simply going to mention a very few of the things which the government and the department are doing to provide transportation facilities to assist in the development of the country because, as anybody who has studied the history of Canada knows only too well, in a country of this size the provision of transportation facilities must precede development. A country of this magnitude must have roads, must have seaways, must have railways and so on before the country can be developed properly, and it is the job of the Department of Transport to provide these facilities.
First of all, in the Atlantic provinces we are carrying out a survey of transportation problems to find out how we can provide better transportation facilities in that region. We are examining the coastal service in Newfoundland to see if the service can be improved over and above what is and has been provided for some years past. We have already decided to provide three new coastal ships, with a possibility of a fourth. We are also planning the new terminal facilities which I mentioned in the house earlier this


year. When the William Carson resumes service from North Sydney to Port aux Basques we will examine the service to see if it fills the needs of Newfoundland for a service to the mainland. If it does not we will then examine into what further facilities might be needed for that service. In conjunction with Canadian National Railways we are studying to see if improvements can be made in the rail service generally throughout Newfoundland.
In Prince Edward Island we are studying to find out whether future requirements are for additional ferry services or if a causeway would provide a better connection to the island. In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia we are studying, in conjunction with Canadian National Railways, to determine how rail services in these two provinces might be improved. We are also reviewing subsidy payments under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. With regard to rail line extensions

I wonder whether the
minister would permit a question before he goes on. Could he tell the house when this study of transportation in the Atlantic provinces was undertaken?
I would say shortly after we took office in June of 1957.
Is it not true that it was undertaken by the previous administration immediately after the presentation of the preliminary Gordon report?
If it was, Mr. Speaker, it was done in such an insignificant way that it really did not start to have any effect until the Conservative government took over.
The minister's memory is failing.

As I was saying before I was interrupted, as far as rail line extensions are concerned, a survey was completed in March of this year and the work of construction has now started on a spur line running from Optic lake to Chisel lake in Manitoba, a distance of 52 miles. It will cost $8,500,000 and will link up properties of the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company with the Hudson Bay Railway. As has been mentioned tonight by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, we are studying at this very moment the proposed new railway line in northern Alberta, a line which will be over 400 miles long and is estimated to cost well over $65 million exclusive of terminal facilities.
With regard to the seaway, in conjunction with various cities with harbours on the seaway we are studying what their needs will be as a consequence of the seaway and have

already entered into arrangements with such cities as Hamilton, Port Arthur and Fort William, Three Rivers and others to see what we can do to help them provide better facilities to be able to handle the traffic which it is confidently expected will develop with the completion of that inland waterway. Recently we sent a team to Kingston from the public works and transport departments to see about additional dredging there to make it possible for ships to pass easily into the excellent harbour of Kingston.
So far as airport construction is concerned, this year we are budgeting for an expenditure of $61 million compared with $35 million budgeted by the late Liberal government in their budget of March 31, 1957. This greatly expanded program, a program almost double that undertaken by the former Liberal government, will include new and enlarged air terminal buildings, additional runways and the lengthening and reinforcing of runways to handle the faster and heavier aircraft which will be appearing in our airways during the next few years. This will, of course, greatly assist exploration and the development of our resources. The new air fields we are building will in many instances be used by exploration companies which fly over otherwise inaccessible stretches of our northland examining areas where it is believed there are mineral resources, thereby making it possible for ground crews to make much more detailed inspections on the ground and actually locate the ores which we believe are there.
With regard to steamship construction, our program this year will cost $22 million compared with a mere $9 under the former government a year ago. This program includes the building of icebreakers and supply ships, all of which will make it possible for navigation to move more easily in icebound waters and will greatly assist the development of our northern areas by making it easier to bring in supplies, equipment and the many other things that are needed for development work in the northern part of our country.
And all this prepared by the Liberal administration.

All of this was not prepared by the Liberal administration. I have quoted to you what the late lamented Liberal administration put in their last budget and I have told you what we have put in our budget. So far as airport construction is concerned, our program is nearly double and in steamship construction it is more than double. Our whole program is vastly increased over anything the Liberal government thought of or
National Development Policy contemplated and it has been thought out and put into operation by the Conservative government.
Would the minister permit a question?
Certainly.
Would the minister be kind enough to give a break-down listing the ships they are going to build during this fiscal year.

I would be very glad to answer on my estimates or the hon. member might like to have some of his Liberal colleagues on the transport committee ask this question. I would be very glad to answer. There is no secret. It is all there to be seen. In fact, we are very proud to talk about it. It is only the modesty of the Conservative government that makes us not bring these things out each time we stand up but if you want to know about them we will be glad to let you know in great and minute detail.
These are the only remarks I intended to make tonight. I did want to mention these things in view of what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said this afternoon when he tried to create the impression that only under a Liberal government were development plans formulated and put into operation. As you will have decided I feel sure, having listened to the very able speech delivered by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, quite the reverse is true. National development was neglected for 22 years under the Liberal government, and under the Conservative government of today quite the reverse is taking place. A national development policy is being put into operation. It is going to develop this country in the manner it has been waiting to be developed for over a generation.

And the gross national
product is going down.

Just as the first great Conservative prime minister recognized only too well, and just as our present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) recognizes so clearly, you must provide transportation facilities in this country to make development possible. This government is going to provide those facilities.
Under the first great Conservative prime minister, the Canadian Pacific railway was built against the vitriolic attacks of the Liberal opposition of that day. The Liberals of that day looked upon development in somewhat the same light as the late Liberal government did. Today, fortunately, we have another great Conservative Prime Minister, who sees development as the most important facet of any government's policy. The policy

National Development Policy of this government, so far as providing transportation facilities is concerned, is simply this. We examine every possible need for the provision of additional transportation facilities. We will continue to do so. Whenever a need can be demonstrated and the fulfilment of that need can be shown to be economically feasible, additional transportation facilities will be provided by this government.
Will the modest and resourceful Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) permit me to ask him a question?
With great pleasure.

What would be his comment about this statement concerning Canada's development which appeared in a 1956 issue of Fortune magazine? They said:
Canada's progress during the past dozen years is one of the economic marvels of the age. Thanks to the extraordinarily high and well-distributed volume of investment, public and private, she has undergone an all-around development not matched even by that of the United States.
I would be very grateful to the minister if he would tell me whether or not he agrees with that statement.
I would simply say that that is evidence of the fact that one of Cockfield Brown's writers had an article accepted by that magazine.
I should like to know if the minister would permit another question?
Yes, with great pleasure.
Is this fortune telling, too?

No, this has nothing to do with fortune telling. I wonder when the minister is going to be just as generous, just as lavish with his grants for shipbuilding, his subventions for the assistance of shipping facilities on the west coast as he has just indicated he is on the east coast?
I believe one of the hallmarks of this government is that we are equally fair with all the ten provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I feel quite sure that no Canadian, either of a previous or present generation, has ever really doubted the remarkable future that is in store for Canada. I do not believe that anyone who knows Canada or has lived here has ever underestimated the economic potential of our great country, with its vast, fertile lands, its industrious, ingenious and reasonable people, as well as the abundance of natural resources which providence has bestowed on our land. I feel quite sure that with all these things in Canada we will
[Mr. Hees.l

be able to realize the vision which Sir Wilfrid Laurier had in the early part of this century when he foresaw that the twentieth century would belong to Canada. I am safe in saying that no one will deny that the first half of the twentieth century has indeed belonged to Canada. We have every reason to expect that if the administration of this country remains sound, the second half of this century will equally belong to Canada.
This will happen under a Conservative government.

I think this leads one to have a justifiable pride in our country. I believe it is significant also that a great number of nations in the world have looked with envy on our great land. They have not looked upon it with envy merely because of the beauty or fertility of our landscape, nor because of the abundance of our natural resources. They have looked upon our country with envy because we have been able to maintain a stable economy in the past. This afternoon I was very pleased to hear the members of parliament from Nigeria, who are now visiting Ottawa, tell me that they thought one of the best things they could say about Canada was that we were not taken in by our tremendous resources. We were able to administer our country wisely and seriously without going to any extremes. We have maintained our stable economy. This we have done in spite of the growing pains from which every young nation must suffer, and in spite of the very heavy war commitments as well as the difficult task of rehabilitating and expanding our industry. We have done this in spite of the increasing demand for social and national security; in spite of economic depressions and recessions, such as the one through which we are now going. The economic stability of our country has indeed been the envy of the world for the past 25 years.
There are reasons why we have been able to administer the country with stability in spite of the pressure that has been put on the government in the past, either from external sources in the field of national security or from internal sources from demands for increased national development. In the past it has been Canada's policy to make sure that she could walk before she tried to run; to make sure also that every step forward was not only desirable and justifiable under economic conditions prevailing, but also that she would not be obliged to take a step backward.
I agree with all members of this house and all Canadians that Canada's true economic potentiality is as yet undreamed of. But I also believe that that economic potentiality

is possible only on certain conditions. The first is that the people of Canada must continue to believe in the elementary and basic principles of the natural law which is that you do not get anything for nothing; you must earn it. Just as whatever accomplishments have been made in the past half century in Canada are due to the efforts and even to the sacrifices of the Canadian people, so are we now moulding the type of future that we are going to leave to future generations. We can either make that future great or we can spoil it. It is within the hands of the Canadian people to mould that future, and it is not easily done.
The second condition-and it is an important one

is that the administration of this country must be based on sound economic principles, with the country's interest as its only objective. There again, this is something which is not always easy of achievement nor is it something which is generally understood throughout the country. But I say that any administration that frames its policy in order to achieve political prestige or popularity alone can indeed jeopardize our whole economic potentiality.
A third condition, I would say, is that we as Canadians must not waste one particle of our national resources, no matter how fabulous or how widespread they may be. I maintain that we must exploit our natural resources systematically and to the fullest possible extent at all times, and that we must not act like spoiled children who, out of greed, take a bit out of several pieces of candy without having either the appetite or the capacity of finishing one. It seems to me that although we have a great economic potentiality we must earn it and that it can be achieved only through reasonable and sound administration.
No one man, or no one political party has the monopoly on the hopes and aspirations for and the faith in Canada's future. Although we all believe in this future, we in this house have differences of opinion as to how best we can achieve this worth-while aim. Recently we have heard a great deal about the largely publicized Conservative vision. It has been presented to Canadians as something completely new, something completely original. Yet it is a vision that has been held by Canadians ever since confederation. This Conservative vision is an indication that the Conservatives are only now discovering Canada and are seeing our country's future.
We discovered Canada a long time ago, much longer ago than you did.

Of course it is a good thing for the government to be forward looking, but it also has its dangers because, blinded
National Development Policy by the vision and blinded by the greatness of our great future-and I am speaking more particularly of the north-and with the inexperienced energy of the neophyte, this government may well try to run before it is sure it can walk on its own two feet without stumbling backwards. On first looking at this Conservative national development program and at these remarkable speeches on northern development at this particular time and under these particular circumstances I cannot help having a vision and it is a vision of a small child biting into huge pieces of new candy but without having finished or digested the several pieces that it already has in hand.
Is that what your leader meant this morning when he said "Look ahead"?

If you take a closer look at the development program brought out by the Conservative party you get the impression that the northern vision may indeed remain in the realm of future possibilities but that the northern development program itself is definitely an illusion.
Hon. members will recall that the national development program that we hear so much about now was introduced not during the last session, at a time when unemployment! was prevalent and at a time when the immediate expenditure of public money might have been indeed useful in checking this unemployment and this recession; oh, no, the development program was not introduced at that time. The government waited until parliament had been prorogued, and immediately afterwards they made this program known. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) kicked off the last election campaign with his national development program.
I am now embarking on a new subject, Mr. Speaker, and I wonder whether I might call it ten o'clock.
